Historical Phases of Russian Orthodoxy The adoption of Orthodoxy by Vladimir the Grand Prince of Kiev marked the starting point of the Christian cycle in Russian history which spans almost the entire history of Russia with the exception of the Soviet period and the era of liberal reforms This cycle represents a complex and multidimensional process which would be inaccurate to describe as a gradual and unidirectional penetration of Orthodox Byzantine culture into the folk environment simultaneously displacing pre Christian pagan beliefs Rather it involved various phases of an extended synthesis of Byzantinism with the East Slavic civilisation of Demetra with these phases being defined by different ratios of the main structures the Byzantine ideology at the elite level and the reception of Christianity by the people as such The following phases defined by various configurations of this ratio can be identified The beginning of the synthesis and the formation of the core of Russian Christian beliefs 10th 12th centuries Kievan centralism The primary differentiation in the formation of the Russian Orthodox tradition depending on the poles of the fracturing Russian world 12th 13th centuries The formation of two poles of Orthodox tradition in the Mongol era Vladimir Moscow Rus and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania 13th 15th centuries The formation of Moscow Orthodoxy Moscow The Third Rome 15th 16th centuries Attempts at purification of Orthodoxy from pagan accretions the circle of devotees of God modernisation and schism 17th century Modernist Orthodoxy Western Russian influence and the parallel establishment of Old Believers in the Russian Empire of the 18th century Slavophilism and Orthodox conservatism elderhood revival of Byzantinism end of the 18th 19th century Sophiology religious searches of the Silver Age figures and projects of unity of faith end of the 19th beginning of the 20th century Persecution and marginalisation of the Church in the Soviet period 1917 1991 The abolition of the normative atheistic ideology and partial return to Orthodoxy during the liberal reforms and the first decades of the 3rd millennium Each of these historical periods had its own semantics and place in the overall structure of Russian history With it the ratio of popular faith to official ideology changed creating a unique configuration of proportions of Russian Orthodoxy in each phase The first phase was characterised by a relatively free relationship between Christian and pre Christian elements where elites including the Orthodox clergy headed by the Byzantine episcopate and more broadly Greek teachers generally tolerated folk beliefs and resorted to repression only when pagans directly challenged the new religion calling for an uprising against it and a return to polytheism This tolerance allowed the initial core of Russian Orthodoxy to form building deep structures of semantic correspondences and homologies between the Indo European yet predominantly peasant tradition of the ancient Slavs and the Christian religion in its Byzantine articulation In the second phase this worldview which had broadly formed and was unified across all ends of Kievan Rus began to partially diverge mirroring the political geography of princely fragmentation at the cultural level However the homology between the religious and the political was partial and relative and the religious cultural community generally prevailed over the gradual distancing of Western Galician Volhynian and Polotsk Rus from the strengthening Eastern Rostov Suzdal later Vladimir Rus as well as over a certain separation of Northern Rus Novgorod and Pskov Nevertheless already in this period a stylistic division between the two poles of Russian Orthodoxy Western and Eastern began to emerge albeit very tentatively and almost imperceptibly Western Orthodoxy was more influenced by neighbouring Catholic peoples primarily Poles and Hungarians as well as directly by Rome than Vladimir Rus which remained more closely connected not just with Byzantium but with the core of Russian Orthodoxy that had formed in the first phase It can be said that the centre of Russian Orthodox tradition had already begun to shift eastward in this phase During the Mongol era the division noted in the second phase became even more pronounced as Eastern and Western Rus found themselves in the context of two different political entities the Golden Horde and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania which united with Catholic Poland after the Union of Krewo If the Mongols whose rulers after Khan Uzbek c 1283 1341 converted to Islam were tolerant or at least indifferent to the Orthodoxy of their Russian subjects then Catholic Poland on the contrary tried to actively influence the Russian population and its religious beliefs This further exacerbated the differences but nonetheless did not lead to the loss of deep unity Meanwhile in Western Rus the official ideology of the elites more easily approached Catholicism whereas the popular peasant masses remained staunch adherents of specifically Orthodox tradition which predetermined a particular tension in this zone of the Russian world between the official ideology and the worldview of the common people In Eastern Rus during the Mongol period such stratification did not occur which became fully evident in the next phase The fourth phase was particularly pronounced in Moscow Rus where after the end of the Golden Horde s dominance a new ideology emerged the Russian Katechon Moscow The Third Rome when the fall of Byzantium and almost simultaneous disappearance of the Golden Horde were perceived as the transfer of the mission of the bulwark of universal Orthodoxy to the Russian state and the Russian people Here the peculiarity of Russian Orthodoxy in its foundational previously Kievan and preserved in Eastern Rus form was recognised as a testimony to eschatological election Something similar we encounter somewhat earlier among the Bulgarians in the First and Second Kingdoms and in the Serbian state of the Nemanjics especially in the era of Du an the Mighty 1308 1355 as well as partly in Wallachia under Vlad III 1431 1476 and Moldavia under Stephen the Great 1429 1504 In this phase especially in the era of Ivan IV 1530 1584 a harmonisation of popular and official Christianity occurs repeating on a new level the synthesis of the elite and the people of the early Kiev period Here not only does Christian consciousness reach the deepest depths of popular culture but the popular spirit rises to the highest peaks of state power affecting the personality of the sovereign himself who became the first Russian tsar in history previously the supreme ruler of the Russian state was the grand prince During the period that includes the Time of Troubles and the reign of the first Romanov tsars the strong cultural and religious cohesion that Moscow enjoyed under Ivan the Terrible began to fade A pivotal group in this era was the Bogolyubsky circle which included central figures of the looming religious division Patriarch Nikon 1605 1681 and Protopope Avvakum 1620 1682 both orbiting around Alexei Mikhailovich 1629 1676 This group aimed to cleanse Christianity of its syncretic folk traditions but their efforts were interpreted differently by two camps those advocating reform and modernisation along the lines of a Western Russian model primarily to facilitate the reintegration of Western Russian territories previously lost to Poland and the Old Believers who rallied behind Avvakum staunchly defending traditional Moscow Orthodoxy as the essence of Russia s divine mission and its role as the guardian of true Orthodoxy These conflicting visions led to a schism within the Russian Orthodox Church The reformists who had gained the upper hand among the elite pursued modernisation efforts far beyond what Nikon had originally envisioned In contrast the Old Belief gained traction among the general populace without however securing a decisive majority largely because of severe state repression In this contentious atmosphere the newly dominant neo ritualism increasingly rejected popular Orthodoxy while the Old Believers endeavoured to preserve the Moscow style of Orthodoxy transforming it into a form of conservative ideology The Old Believers attributed Nikon s departure from traditional practices and his followers actions to Western Russian influences thus adding a geopolitical layer to the religious disputes that had been evident since the era of principality fragmentation In the sixth phase of Russian Orthodoxy s evolution the changes initiated by the schism continued to unfold After Peter the Great there was a significant shift in Orthodox tradition towards modernism This shift was no longer predominantly influenced by the Western Russian or partially Greek traditions as during Nikon s reforms Instead it directly embraced Western European influences where Catholic and Protestant themes became markedly more pronounced This period was marked by an increasing secularisation and a growing divide between the ruling aristocracy and the general populace The peasantry was marginalised and treated more as an economic asset than a part of society with rights and voices In response to these changes Old Belief found renewed vigour among the common people and numerous new sects emerged reflecting apocalyptic and ecstatic beliefs These sects either directly or indirectly presented a challenge to the established Orthodox Church This era saw a resurgence of pre Christian motifs preserved by Old Believers in a Christianised form which surfaced in new and often grotesque expressions among Russian sectarians Interestingly during this time what could be considered Western Russian Orthodoxy appeared more conservative in comparison to the modernist and secular trends that dominated the post Petrine 18th century adding another layer of complexity to the religious landscape of Russia From the end of the 18th century a reverse process gradually unfolded Russian Orthodoxy in its popular Byzantine Moscow dimension gradually regained its position in Russian society as a whole This process was associated with the revival of elderhood and Athos hesychasm parallel in Moldavia and Russia and somewhat later with the Slavophile movement which criticised modernisation and Europeanisation of the Petrine era and called for a return to the ideals of Moscow Rus and the corresponding worldview uniting the two parts of Russian society the Westernised but still monarchical and nominally Orthodox elite and the Russian people peasantry Thus for the third time this time as a project and reflection on the historical religious fate of the Russian people an attempt at religious synthesis of the ruling elite and the common people occurred Gradually Slavophilism became almost the official ideology of the tsarist regime and inspired the culture of the Russian Golden Age Symbolically the unity of faith proposing to unite the Old Belief and the official church hierarchy was established exactly in 1800 thus marking a milestone in Russian religious history Following the Slavophiles the issue of folk religiosity its relationship with official Orthodoxy and the state became the focus of attention during the Silver Age of Russian culture Vladimir Solovyov 1853 1900 the founder of Russian religious philosophy attempted to understand the uniqueness of Russian Orthodoxy and its relationship with the Russian state universal Christianity and the history of European societies This led to an important thesis on the concept of sophia or Holy Wisdom as the key to understanding Russian identity and Russia s mission in world history During this period figures of the Russian Silver Age and leading representatives of sophiology such as V Rozanov 1856 1919 P Florensky 1882 1937 S Bulgakov 1871 1944 N Berdyaev 1874 1948 D Merezhkovsky 1865 1941 A Blok 1880 1921 A Bely 1880 1934 Vyach Ivanov 1866 1949 and others often ventured beyond the boundaries of Orthodox orthodoxy connecting with some folk sectarian movements such as the Khlysts Skoptsy etc This eighth phase questioned Orthodoxy itself in its relation to Western Christianity K Leontiev 1831 1891 V Solovyov D Merezhkovsky etc the peculiarities of the Russian Orthodox tradition P Florensky S Bulgakov V Rozanov N Berdyaev etc and the differences even opposition between the ideological foundations of the Russian people and the Russian state most fully developed in the works of Leo Tolstoy 1828 1910 as well as among the populists and later the socialist revolutionaries The common people as the number of intelligentsia grew and public education spread gradually joined this dialogue along with the aristocracy creating a unique situation in Russian history where common folk actively engaged in addressing philosophical questions Prominent examples of such inclusion are Russian poets Nikolai Klyuev 1884 1937 Sergey Yesenin 1895 1925 Velimir Khlebnikov 1885 1922 and to some extent Vladimir Mayakovsky 1893 1930 As the Russian people sought their own identity including the religious aspect and as tsarist state power weakened this quest took on radical forms ultimately leading to the Bolsheviks seizing power The Bolsheviks in line with their ideology aimed to eradicate Christianity attempting to eliminate both Orthodoxy and all forms of religion However as noted by Berdyaev the Eurasianists and the National Bolsheviks Russian Bolshevism beneath its formal atheism materialism and Marxism contained eschatological motifs of Russian sectarianism reflecting the most archaic depths of Russian identity In this context the most ancient layers of Russian identity not just pre Christian but sometimes Paleo European and matriarchal tracing back to the Trypillian culture were awakened In the tenth phase Russian Orthodoxy including both the new ritualists and the Old Believers as well as actual sectarianism became a target of deliberate repression However when these repressions eased from the early years of the Great Patriotic War it existed on the fringes of society having virtually no impact on the predominantly Communist worldview shared by most of the Soviet population Remarkably even in this phase the core of Orthodox tradition was preserved at least in the form it existed before the Bolshevik Revolution The intensive implementation of the Soviet materialist scientific worldview did not go without consequences and even within the Orthodox community natural scientific materialism and ideas of progress and development infiltrated Their incompatibility with fully fledged Christianity was emphatically highlighted by sophiologists When the USSR collapsed and the doctrines of atheism lost their normative status Orthodoxy began to reclaim its position in Russia The anti communism of the liberal reformers of the 1990s was initially quite aggressive towards the Orthodox Church viewing it as a reactionary institution hindering social progress and the modernisation and Westernisation of Russian society However as communism was the primary adversary systematic repressions against Orthodoxy did not materialise The Orthodox Church used this opportunity to strengthen its influence in society becoming especially noticeable from the early 2000s Yet this time Orthodoxy did not reflect either the ideology of the ruling elite or the natural worldview of the masses which had been fundamentally influenced by Soviet education This led to uncertainty and insecurity about which phase to use as a model for a church wide revival All nine previous moments in Russia s religious history had different structures and orientations Consequently this question remains open today and the current tenth phase is an extended resolution of this fundamental issue Practically all positions are represented in contemporary Russian society especially considering the religious processes unfolding in the western part of the Russian world in Ukraine and Belarus Thus in modern Orthodoxy one can find modernists progressives natural scientific materialists evolutionists fundamentalists of the Moscow period sometimes proclaiming the necessity of canonising Ivan the Terrible ideologues of Old Belief actors of the unity of faith revival sophiologists Eurasianists National Bolsheviks justifying Stalin and aligned with Patriarch Sergius stance extreme anti communists both monarchists and liberals those inclined towards Gnosticism and sectarianism Uniates especially characteristic of Western Rus ecumenists advocating the unification of Orthodoxy with Western Christian denominations narrow nationalists Pan Slavists traditionalists seeking a common platform with believers of other religions in opposition to modernisation secularisation and postmodernism conformists ready to accept any ideology purists insisting on the purity of Orthodoxy and a wide variety of sectarians None of these versions dominantly prevails and the overall structure of the tenth phase in which contemporary Russian society lives cannot be definitively determined However to understand this tenth phase it is necessary to correctly analyse and comprehend all previous ones as it results Constantinople in 559 settled north of the Danube and were absorbed by the Avars Following the collapse of Avar power in the eighth century new Bulgar arrivals and existing elites in Transdanubia gradually formed the Bulgar khanate which adopted Slavic language and customs Given their cultural origins in the Eurasian steppe it is unsurprising that throughout the medieval period the Bulgarian social elite fought mostly as heavy armed cavalry lancers Bulgaria formed the most important state to the north of the empire Though there were long stretches of peace between the two peoples and even alliance Byzantine Bulgar relations were strained by their fundamental conflicting goals both empires sought to dominate the Balkans and each considered presence of the other unacceptable Thus the Bulgars sought to capture Constantinople or subjugate the Byzantines militarily while the latter sought to contain or even annex Bulgaria outright Initially the Bulgars organized themselves along the lines of most steppe empires with inner and outer tribes whose power relationships were articulated through marriage alliances genealogies and material exchange Beneath the outer tribes in the pecking order were subject groups like Slavs Greeks and the m lange of Avar Hunnic and Germanic remnants that rendered the rich cultural matrix of the Danube basin The khan stood at the pinnacle of an increasingly sophisticated hierarchy that developed under steppe and Byzantine influence Senior inner nobles called boilas often Anglicized as boyar and junior outer nobles bagains formed the elite of the Bulgar state and provided both the military leadership and elite troops of the khanate The Bulgars matched their Byzantine foe with a strong hierarchical military organization with the khan in overall command while his leading generals the tarqan commanded his administrative regional center and presumably took the center of the battle line as well The targan s subordinates included komites sing komes after Byzantine usage who commanded the wings of the army The highest ranking Bulgar nobles were heavily equipped cavalry with barded mounts and relied on heavy household cavalry and lighter armed horse archers as did their steppe nomad ancestors Bulgars employed mass conscription to fill out the ranks for their armies Fear was the main tool used to compel men to enlist and show up equipped for the occasion Khan Boris Michael d 907 ordered that men who arrived for muster without proper equipment or unprepared for campaign were to be executed as were those who deserted before or during battle The rank and file included many Slavs who fought as light infantry carrying shields and javelins Bulgar cavalry resembled both their Byzantine enemy and other steppe nomads The Bulgars were expert in their use of terrain relying on ambush and surprise in their confrontation with the enemy They demonstrated a high level of strategic planning strong discipline and military cohesion and on numerous occasions were able to confront and defeat imperial field armies as they did at Varbica in 811 when they trapped a large force led by the emperor Nikephoros I and destroyed it by hemming the Byzantines against a wooden palisade and surrounding it Emperor himself was killed and his heir mortally wounded Bulgars were intimately acquainted with Byzantine military strategy and The Basilica Cistern A Treasured Secret Under Istanbul T rkiye Beneath the bustling streets of Istanbul lies the Basilica Cistern a remarkable testament to Byzantine ingenuity Constructed in the 6th century CE under the reign of Emperor Justinian I 527 565 CE this vast underground reservoir was designed to supply water to Great Palace of Constantinople and nearby buildings Measuring approximately 140m in length and 70m in width it has the capacity to store around 80 000 cubic meters of water showcasing the advanced hydraulic engineering of the Byzantine Empire Among the 336 graceful marble columns that support the cistern two are particularly noteworthy the mysterious Medusa heads one resting upside down and the other on its side Scholars have long speculated about the reasoning behind this unusual positioning some suggest it was a deliberate choice rooted in mythology intended to counteract Medusa s legendary ability to turn onlookers to stone while others argue it simply reflects the practical reuse of materials from older Roman structures After the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople in 1453 the cistern fell into a period of neglect and became largely forgotten until its rediscovery in 1545 by the French traveler Petrus Gyllius He uncovered it after locals spoke of drawing water and even fish from their wells Today the Basilica Cistern has emerged as a popular tourist attraction where history legend and architectural marvels converge providing visitors with a haunting yet captivating insight into the rich heritage of Istanbul

Republics of Pisa Genoa and Venice were firmly established Amalfi traders were already navigating the waters and trading throughout the Mediterranean At this time town s small harbor was full of sailing vessels that crisscrossed sea reaching ports as far as Egypt Syria and Constantinople in Byzantine Empire Amalfi had its own gold currency called the Tar which was used in ports throughout Mediterranean Africa Greek Empire and East Amalfi s influence on seas is well documented in Tabula Amalphitana or Amalfi Tables which established a maritime code that used throughout Mediterranean until 1570 Amalfi remained a rich and powerful Republic until 1073 when it fell under Norman control Power was shifting in Mediterranean to Republics of Pisa and Genoa both of which were eager to secure their territory Amalfi suffered two damaging attacks by Pisans in 1135 and again two years later Despite these setbacks Amalfi thrived intellectually and creatively during 12th 13th Centuries Paradise 1268 and Romanesque Moorish style Campanile 1180 1276 Thanks to trading connections with East by about 1230s Amalfi became one of the first locations in Europe to produce paper Sitting at the base of a ravine with a fresh water source running down Valle dei Mulini Valley of Mills Amalfi was an ideal setting for paper making Mills were powered by the cool mountain water and Amalfi s paper was soon sold all over the Mediterranean Paper making continued as an important local trade throughout the Middle Ages and Renaissance Today you can visit the ruins of the original mills as well as learn more about the history of paper making in Amalfi at the Museo della Carta Paper Museum Amalfi s period of prosperity changed drastically in the 14th century when town succumbed to the plague in came under the rule of the nearby Kingdom of Naples in late 14th Century Lacking military and trading influence town slowly returned to a sleepy fishing village By 19th Century travellers from throughout Europe began to rediscover the history and beauty of the Naples area on the Grand Tour The wild and seemingly untouched beauty of Amalfi Coast spoke to romantic spirit of these travellers who found inspiration in scenes of daily life evocative architecture and natural landscape Writers poets musicians and painters arriving on Amalfi Coast were stunned by its natural beauty American poet Henry Longfellow arrived in 1869 and later wrote a poem entitled Amalfi 1875 inspired by his time in the small fishing village Amalfi Coast remained isolated geographically until 19th Century when Ferdinand II Bourbon King of Naples commissioned construction of a road connecting villages dotting the coastline Amalfi Coast road reached Amalfi by middle of century and this provided access that today allows countless tourists each year to experience beauty of Amalfi Coast

PALESTINE AN ANCIENT GEOGRAPHIC NAME BUT NOT A PRE EXISTING SOVEREIGN ARAB STATE The claim that an independent country called Palestine existed for centuries before being replaced by Israel in 1948 is not supported by the administrative or diplomatic record Palestine unquestionably existed as a geographic designation Palestinian Arabs unquestionably developed a modern national identity But geography peoplehood and sovereign statehood are three different historical questions Confusing them produces political slogans instead of serious analysis Before the modern period the territory between the Mediterranean Sea and the Jordan River was governed by kingdoms empires caliphates and colonial administrations It was never ruled as an independent sovereign state by a Palestinian Arab national government THE ANCIENT NAME Forms of the name Palestine are ancient Greek writers used terms derived from Palaistin for part of the eastern Mediterranean coast After suppressing the Bar Kokhba revolt in the second century CE Roman authorities incorporated Judaea into the province commonly known as Syria Palaestina The renaming is frequently interpreted as an attempt to weaken the territory s association with Jewish Judaea although historians debate the exact administrative motives and timing What is certain is that Syria Palaestina was a Roman province not an independent Palestinian nation state Under Byzantine rule the region was divided into provinces called Palaestina Prima Palaestina Secunda and Palaestina Tertia These names preserved a geographic and administrative designation under imperial authority The ancient Philistines from whom the geographic name ultimately derived were not the direct national predecessors of the modern Arabic speaking Palestinian population Similarity of name does not establish uninterrupted political sovereignty or ethnic identity across thousands of years ISLAMIC RULE A DISTRICT NOT A COUNTRY Muslim armies conquered the region from the Byzantine Empire during the seventh century Early Islamic governments established Jund Filastin the military district of Palestine within the larger province of Bilad al Sham Jund Filastin had administrative centers first at Lydda and later Ramla Jerusalem became one of Islam s most important religious cities but the district did not operate as an independent state It remained subordinate to successive caliphates headquartered elsewhere Its boundaries also differed from those associated with modern Palestine Galilee and parts of the north belonged at various times to Jund al Urdunn the district of Jordan The use of Filastin therefore demonstrates the continuity of a regional name It does not demonstrate the existence of sovereign Palestinian statehood The same distinction applies under later Crusader Ayyubid and Mamluk governments The land remained strategically and religiously important but it was governed as part of larger political systems THE OTTOMAN PERIOD The Ottoman Empire controlled the region from 1516 until Britain s conquest during the First World War The Ottomans did not maintain a single sovereign or autonomous province corresponding exactly to Mandate Palestine During the empire s final decades Jerusalem and its surrounding territory formed a specially administered district reporting directly to Istanbul Northern areas were administered through districts connected to Beirut while other territories were attached to different provincial structures There was no independent Palestinian executive national legislature foreign ministry or army exercising sovereignty over the territory Local Arab families possessed substantial municipal commercial and religious influence but they operated within the Ottoman imperial system This does not mean the local Arab population lacked attachment to its towns land or region Ottoman subjects could possess local religious Arab and Syrian identities simultaneously Modern nationalism had not yet imposed the exclusive categories that dominate today s conflict THE BRITISH MANDATE WAS NOT PALESTINIAN INDEPENDENCE Following the First World War the League of Nations entrusted Britain with the Mandate for Palestine The Mandate formally recognized the Jewish people s historical connection to the land and committed Britain to facilitating the establishment of a Jewish national home while protecting the civil and religious rights of the non Jewish population Britain remained the governing authority Mandate Palestine was therefore an internationally established territorial administration not an independent Palestinian Arab state The word Palestinian was geographical during much of this period It could refer to Arab and Jewish inhabitants of the Mandate Institutions including the Palestine Post and Palestine Symphony Orchestra were established by Jews while Palestinian Arab newspapers political committees and organizations increasingly used the same regional identity for Arab national purposes Palestinian Arab nationalism did not suddenly appear in 1967 Its foundations emerged during the late Ottoman and British Mandate periods and strengthened through opposition to Zionism British policy and increasing Jewish immigration The wars of 1948 and 1967 consolidated that identity but they did not create it from nothing A national identity can be real even when it has not previously produced an independent sovereign state 1947 AND THE STATE THAT WAS NOT ESTABLISHED In November 1947 the United Nations proposed partitioning the Mandate into independent Arab and Jewish states with a special international arrangement for Jerusalem The Jewish leadership accepted partition as a basis for statehood despite serious reservations Arab leaders rejected the plan arguing that it violated the rights of the Arab majority and unfairly awarded territory to the proposed Jewish state Israel declared independence on May 14 1948 Neighboring Arab armies entered the former Mandate beginning the first Arab Israeli war When the fighting ended no Palestinian Arab state had been established Jordan controlled and later annexed the West Bank and East Jerusalem Egypt administered the Gaza Strip but did not annex it or transform it into a genuinely sovereign Palestinian state The All Palestine Government proclaimed in Gaza in 1948 possessed limited authority and depended heavily upon Egypt It never exercised effective sovereignty over the territory proposed for the Arab state From 1949 until 1967 Jordan and Egypt controlled the territories most commonly envisioned as the foundation of a Palestinian state Neither created one MODERN PALESTINIAN STATEHOOD The Palestine Liberation Organization was established in 1964 In 1988 the Palestinian National Council declared the State of Palestine The Oslo process later created the Palestinian Authority which exercises limited and divided governmental functions in parts of the West Bank Hamas has separately controlled Gaza since 2007 In 2012 the United Nations General Assembly granted Palestine non member observer state status The State of Palestine is recognized diplomatically by a large majority of UN members although it is not a full UN member and does not exercise complete unified sovereignty over its claimed territory This modern reality makes the absolute statement there has never been a country called Palestine too broad Palestine now possesses significant international recognition and participates in international institutions as a state The historically defensible argument is narrower Before the twentieth century conflict there was no independent sovereign Palestinian Arab state from which Israel seized national sovereignty in 1948 WHAT THE RECORD SHOWS Palestine is an ancient geographic name Jewish history sovereignty and continuous connection to the land long predate Islam and modern Arab nationalism Arabic speaking communities lived in the territory for centuries and developed a distinct Palestinian national identity during the modern period The territory was governed successively by larger empires and foreign administrations rather than by an independent Palestinian Arab state Mandate Palestine was a British administered legal territory not a sovereign country A proposed Arab state was not established in 1948 The West Bank and Gaza subsequently came under Jordanian and Egyptian control Modern Palestinian claims to statehood cannot be proven or disproven solely by whether such a state existed previously International statehood is a political and legal question not an inheritance system requiring an ancient predecessor THE DECODE The strongest historical argument does not deny that Palestinians exist It does not need questionable quotations exaggerated claims or the suggestion that every nation must possess an ancient currency or dynasty to have modern political rights The decisive distinction is simpler Palestine existed for centuries as a geographic and administrative name Palestinian Arab identity developed into a modern national movement But there was no independent sovereign Palestinian Arab country governing the land before Israel s establishment in 1948 Recognizing that fact does not resolve the present conflict It corrects a specific historical claim Israel did not replace an already functioning sovereign Palestinian state The past provides both peoples with history It does not automatically give either side an uncontested political settlement in the present That settlement must be argued through security recognition negotiation and law not invented sovereignty projected backward across thousands of years Decode Conflict Historical Assessment Share

as their prize Their animosity culminated in a series of conflicts known as the Civil Wars of the Tetrarchy The Battle of Chrysopolis was the decisive climax The battle was not just a test of military strategy and might It was also a symbolic showdown between the pagan traditions represented by Licinius and the burgeoning Christian faith championed by Constantine Winning this battle didn t merely ruler The ramifications of Chrysopolis echoed through the ages Constantine s sole rule marked the start of a Christian centric governance It paved the way for the Edict of Milan granting religious tolerance to Christians and set the stage for the First Council of Nicaea in 325 AD which aimed to unify Christian teachings The battle also hinted at the future significance of Byzantium which Constantine would refashion into Constantinople the New Rome This city would later become the heart of the Byzantine Empire a Christian bastion standing tall for another millennium In the tapestry of history Chrysopolis shines not just as a military confrontation but as a pivotal juncture A moment when the threads of faith politics and destiny intertwined to shape the course of empires and Unearthing History The Lost Jewish Town of the First Temple Period In an extraordinary archaeological discovery a forgotten Jewish town from the First Temple period was found beneath the ruins of an abandoned military training base near Beit El This remarkable finding has opened a window into the complex layered history of the ancient Levant providing an unprecedented view into a settlement that existed through nearly a thousand years of continuous occupation from early Jewish settlements to Byzantine Christianity The artifacts and structural remnants unearthed at this site not only enrich our understanding of the region s evolving cultures and powers but also reveal how the daily lives of ordinary people unfolded amidst major historical upheavals This town initially founded during the First Temple period was part of the ancient kingdom of Judah Its earliest inhabitants lived under Judean kings in an era marked by significant territorial expansions internal conflicts and alliances with neighboring empires With the Babylonian conquest in the early 6th century BCE this community like many in Judah would have experienced turmoil displacement and eventual resettlement following Babylon s decline and Persia s rise to regional dominance in 539 BCE Under Persian rule the Jewish community enjoyed relative stability as evidenced by the widespread return of exiled populations and the rebuilding of religious institutions including the Second Temple in Jerusalem This town with its close proximity to Jerusalem likely served as a supporting settlement for those making pilgrimages and engaging in commerce with the heart of the Jewish faith Archaeologists found a wide array of artifacts from these early periods including iron tools pottery fragments and intricate stone door keys The iron tools point to a town deeply engaged in agriculture trade and craftsmanship indicative of a thriving self sufficient community The pottery pieces especially those inscribed with seals and Hebrew script add a significant dimension to the settlement s cultural identity reflecting trade networks religious practices and administrative functions within the ancient Judean economy During the Persian era stamped bullae clay seal impressions found on site bear the names and titles of officials signifying a bureaucratic presence and a connection to regional governance Such artifacts underscore the town s administrative role and its integration into the larger administrative apparatus established by the Persian Empire across its territories The settlement continued to develop witnessing control shifts from the Persians to the Greeks following Alexander the Great s conquests in the 4th century BCE It later fell under the influence of the Hasmonean dynasty in the 2nd century BCE a period known for Jewish self governance after the Maccabean Revolt Architectural shifts observed at the site such as fortified walls and evidence of small synagogues point to a distinct Jewish identity resilient in the face of foreign influences and cultural syncretism This resilience is also visible in the burial customs and ceremonial spaces that archaeologists have connected to specific Jewish traditions suggesting that despite political changes the town s inhabitants maintained their religious customs and cultural practices Roman rule established in 63 BCE under Pompey s campaign brought a new chapter of transformation The Romans known for their architectural prowess and infrastructure likely influenced this town s urban planning even as the Jewish population endured growing tensions with their Roman rulers The discovery of Roman coins household items and inscriptions reveals both assimilation and resistance as the Jewish inhabitants navigated the constraints of Roman governance Archaeologists also uncovered remnants of defensive structures and weaponry possibly linked to the various Jewish revolts against Roman rule notably the First Jewish Roman War 66 73 CE These relics highlight the tensions that permeated life in Judean settlements and the enduring spirit of a people determined to preserve their heritage As the Roman Empire transitioned into the Byzantine period Christianity spread throughout the region transforming both the social and religious fabric of Judean communities This town too experienced a significant shift with Jewish traditions gradually giving way to Christian practices By the 5th century CE the once Jewish settlement had become a Christian community complete with newly built monasteries churches and Christian symbols adorning its public spaces The shift is evident from the discovery of crosses religious inscriptions and mosaics that adorned church floors demonstrating the Byzantine influence on the architecture and cultural symbols of the period Monastic communities became prominent with evidence suggesting that these monasteries served as spiritual centers for pilgrims and a base for missionary activities spreading Christianity to the surrounding areas The town s journey through history likely met a sudden end with a catastrophic earthquake in the late 8th century CE Archaeological evidence such as collapsed structures and human remains caught in positions suggesting an attempt to escape points to this natural disaster s violent impact Historical records from the period describe earthquakes that devastated large parts of the Levant and this particular site s ruinous state aligns with these accounts The earthquake s destruction sealed the town s legacy beneath layers of rubble and earth preserving a narrative of resilience adaptation and survival across generations Today this ancient town stands as a testament to the enduring spirit of its inhabitants who lived adapted and thrived despite the sweeping changes that shaped the ancient Near East Each artifact structure and layer of soil excavated from this site adds a piece to the larger puzzle of human history capturing a time when faith culture and power intersected in a region at the heart of ancient civilization Archaeologists continue to study and interpret the site contributing to a more comprehensive understanding of how communities navigated the complexities of life in an era marked by immense change This lost town hidden beneath a now abandoned military base not only reveals the story of a forgotten past but also connects us to the enduring legacy of human resilience and the ever evolving tapestry of cultural heritage

of whose actions extends far beyond it and will be felt to the end of time They have not led armies to the field nor sat in the councils of nations but neither warrior nor statesman has ever done or prosecution of lower aims These aims were always limited to temporal concerns and generally to the furtherance of personal ambition and therefore they were contracted within the span of a single life and were as ephemeral in their influence as they were puny in their conception The mightiest achievements of such men left no permanent mark on the moral face of the world It remained what it was Rabbi Akiva Bar Kochba and the Birth of Palestine The Transformation of Judea in Roman Antiquity The Jewish Roman wars remain one of the most dramatic episodes of ancient history Among the key figures in these times was Rabbi Akiva an influential rabbi and martyr whose life intertwined with the tragic fate of Judea during the second century CE The events that followed the Bar Kochba Revolt a three year uprising from 132 to 135 CE against Roman occupation reshaped not only Jewish life but the very identity of the land itself as Rome took measures to erase Judea from the map replacing it with the name Palestine This renaming marked a turning point in both the historical and symbolic landscape of the region embedding layers of significance that resonate to this day Rabbi Akiva A Man of Faith and Defiance Rabbi Akiva ben Yosef often regarded as one of the foundational figures in Jewish tradition was an unlikely hero Born into humble beginnings perhaps even from a non Jewish background Akiva only began his religious studies in adulthood However he quickly rose to prominence due to his intellect charisma and commitment to Torah study His teachings emphasized the unity of the Jewish people and the importance of preserving Jewish law and identity amid the challenges of Roman rule Akiva s role during the Bar Kochba Revolt is crucial to understanding the intersection of Jewish spiritual leadership and military rebellion Although traditionally rabbis were not directly involved in political struggles Akiva made an exception with Shimon bar Kochba a Jewish leader who claimed messianic aspirations Akiva endorsed him as the Messiah a daring declaration that risked the wrath of Rome and signaled his defiant stance against oppression By doing so he fueled the hope and determination of Jewish fighters Despite his support for Bar Kochba Rabbi Akiva was a pacifist at heart and his support for the rebellion was a profound departure from his teachings Akiva saw in Bar Kochba a chance for redemption and freedom but the rebellion ended in tragedy with Bar Kochba killed in battle and Akiva himself eventually captured and tortured to death by the Romans His martyrdom became a symbol of Jewish endurance and resistance even in the face of overwhelming adversity The Bar Kochba Revolt Final Attempt at Sovereignty The Bar Kochba Revolt was not merely a regional uprising it was the Jewish people s last major attempt to assert sovereignty in their ancestral homeland The revolt emerged in response to Roman Emperor Hadrian s policies particularly his plan to rebuild Jerusalem as a Roman colony named Aelia Capitolina where pagan worship was intended to replace Jewish customs and sacred sites Hadrian s imposition of severe restrictions on Jewish religious practices combined with his desire to erase Jewish identity in the region ignited the revolt Bar Kochba s fighters initially enjoyed success establishing a temporary Jewish state and forcing Roman legions into retreat However Rome was relentless Determined to quash the Jewish resistance Hadrian dispatched one of the largest Roman military forces ever assembled employing scorched earth tactics that devastated the land and decimated the population By 135 CE after years of brutal warfare the rebellion was finally crushed and Judea lay in ruins The death toll was staggering with Roman historian Cassius Dio estimating over half a million Jewish casualties A Symbolic Rewriting The Birth of Palestine In the aftermath of the Bar Kochba Revolt Hadrian took unprecedented steps to erase the memory of Judea from the Roman Empire His aim was not just political it was psychological and cultural Determined to sever the Jewish connection to their homeland he abolished the name Provincia Judaea Judea and instead renamed the region Syria Palaestina This decision was strategic by selecting Palestina a term derived from Philistia the ancient enemies of Israel from the coastal region of Canaan Hadrian sent a message that this land no longer belonged to the Jews He sought to sever the historical and spiritual ties of the Jewish people to the land of their ancestors For the Romans renaming territories was a tool of subjugation a way to demoralize conquered populations and assert the permanence of Roman rule To Roman audiences the name change seemed inconsequential another routine act in the empire s vast portfolio of renamings But for the Jewish people the erasure of Judea was a devastating blow as it symbolized not only their loss of autonomy but also an attempt to erase their very identity from history The New Palestinians From Romans to Byzantine Christians After the renaming those who inhabited Palestina included a mix of remaining Jewish communities Roman colonists Greek speaking Christians and pagans Over the next centuries the Roman Empire evolved into the Byzantine Empire and Palestine became a predominantly Christian territory part of the Christian Byzantine Empire s administrative divisions Jewish populations were further marginalized and a new culture arose that blended Roman Greek and early Christian influences The Jewish connection to the land remained through religious communities in Galilee and through the pilgrims who visited the remains of the Second Temple but they lived under restrictive conditions forbidden to enter Jerusalem except on Tisha B Av the day of mourning for the Temple s destruction Lasting Impact of the Name Palestine in Jewish and Christian Histories The renaming of Judea as Palestine had far reaching consequences that extended beyond the Roman period For Jews the name Palestine would come to represent a period of exile foreign rule and alienation from their homeland Jewish liturgical texts began to reflect this sense of loss with prayers for the return to Zion and the rebuilding of Jerusalem fueling hopes that would endure for nearly two millennia By contrast in the Christian world Palestine became synonymous with the Holy Land As Christianity spread through the Roman Empire and later into Europe Palestine was cherished as the site of Jesus ministry miracles crucifixion and resurrection Christian pilgrims traveled from across the empire to visit the sacred sites and the name Palestine became embedded in Christian maps texts and traditions as a land associated with religious reverence Ironically despite Hadrian s intentions the name Palestine ultimately reinforced rather than erased the Jewish connection to the land For Jewish and Christian communities alike Palestine became a symbol of spiritual longing and the promise of redemption The Legacy of Rabbi Akiva and the Enduring Story of Palestine The legacy of Rabbi Akiva and the transformation of Judea into Palestine represent intertwined histories of faith identity and resilience For Jews the fall of Judea was a traumatic loss yet it laid the foundation for the Jewish diaspora s survival and the preservation of Jewish identity Rabbi Akiva s teachings and martyrdom embodied the spirit of endurance that would sustain the Jewish people throughout centuries of exile The dream of returning to Zion which he championed lived on in Jewish hearts fostering a sense of identity that transcended borders Meanwhile Palestine continued its journey through history shaped by the ebb and flow of empires and religious traditions Although Hadrian sought to erase the Jewish connection to the land his decision to rename Judea as Palestine ultimately created a new historical and cultural layer that preserved memories of the land s past both for Jews and Christians Today the name Palestine remains a potent reminder of the region s complex and multifaceted history Its story rooted in the struggle for The Order of Knights of the Hospital of Saint John of Jerusalem known simply also as the Knights Hospitaller was a religious military order that was founded in Jerusalem during the 11th century AD Although the order was initially established to provide care for poor and sick pilgrims it later took up arms to defend pilgrims and the Holy Land After the fall of the Crusader states the knights relocated and continued their fight against the Muslims The role played by the Knights Hospitallers in the defense of Christendom allowed the order to maintain its relevance long after the Crusades and the Middle Ages The order has survived till this day losing its military role but retaining its original commitment to care for the poor and sick Around 1048 merchants from the Republic of Amalfi in Italy obtained permission from the Fatimid Caliph of Egypt to build a church convent and hospital in the holy city of Jerusalem The hospital was founded on the site of the Monastery of Saint John the Baptist and the task of running it was given to a community of Benedictine monks The monks were to provide care for poor and sick pilgrims who visited the holy city In 1099 the Kingdom of Jerusalem was established following the success of the First Crusade At that time the superior of the hospital was a lay brother by the name of Gerard Under Gerard s guidance the community s work in Jerusalem intensified and more hospitals were founded in Provencal and Italian cities that were along the route to the Holy Land On February 15 1113 a papal bull issued by Pope Paschal II recognized the foundation of the hospital and the order was formally named as the Order of Knights of the Hospital of Saint John of Jerusalem Although the papal bull placed the order under the Church it was free to elect its superiors without interference from either secular or religious authorities The reorganization of the Knights Hospitaller into a military occurred partially due to the rise of the Templars This order was established in 1119 for the protection of pilgrims to the Holy Land and was immensely popular In order to compete with the Templars for support Hospitallers imitated the military role of their rivals which soon paid off Nevertheless the Hospitallers retained their role as care givers As a result the hierarchy of the order consisted of three ranks knights chaplains and serving brothers In 1291 the last major Crusader stronghold in the Holy Land Acre fell to the Mamluks As a consequence the Hospitallers were forced to move their headquarters to Limassol on the island of Cyprus From their new base the knights built up a naval fleet which they used to protect pilgrims who traveled to the Holy Land by sea At that time Cyprus was a Crusader state known as the Kingdom of Cyprus and the knights sought to acquire a state of their own The knights targeted the island of Rhodes which was part of the Byzantine Empire A fleet landed on the island in 1307 and by 1301 the knights were the new masters of the island With their new headquarters on Rhodes the order became known also as the Knights of Rhodes

the Taurus Mountains and the Mediterranean world But Thoros carried another memory with him the memory of a murdered king Gagik II the last Bagratid king of Armenia had been killed by the Greek Mandal medieval period Jews experienced both golden ages of acceptance and dark times of persecution The destruction of the Second Temple in 70 AD by Roman forces marked a pivotal turning point for the Jewish people With the heart of their religious and cultural life in ruins many Jews found themselves displaced from their ancestral homeland This event catalyzed the beginning of a widespread diaspora a dispersal that would see Jewish communities establish themselves in regions far from Jerusalem As they ventured beyond the borders of Judea Jewish communities began to settle in various parts of the Roman Empire including North Africa Asia Minor and Europe Babylon in particular became a significant center for Jewish life and scholarship In subsequent centuries diaspora expanded even in commerce academia and local governance The destruction of the Second Temple left a profound void in the religious and cultural life of the Jewish people Without the central institution that had anchored their worship and rituals there was a pressing need for a new framework to guide Jewish life and ensure continuity of their traditions This vacuum led to emergence of Rabbinic Judaism a transformative movement that would shape the trajectory of Jewish thought and practice for centuries to come At the forefront of this movement were the rabbis learned scholars and teachers who took on mantle of interpreting and preserving Jewish law or Halakha They engaged in rigorous debates discussions and interpretations of Torah seeking to understand its teachings in the context of a rapidly changing world Their deliberations were meticulously recorded leading to compilation of the Mishnah a structured collection of oral traditions and laws This text in turn became the foundation for took on a more central role in religious worship The home became a focal point for religious observance with rituals like the Sabbath dinner and the Passover Seder reinforcing communal bonds and traditions In early medieval period many Jewish communities found themselves under Islamic rule especially after rapid expansion of the Muslim Caliphates Places like Al Andalus in Spain became centers of Jewish intellectual and cultural activity Here Jewish scholars poets and physicians thrived often serving as intermediaries between Muslim and Christian worlds They translated works from Arabic to Latin contributing to preservation and transmission of ancient knowledge The relative tolerance of these Islamic realms allowed Jewish thought to flourish producing luminaries such as Maimonides whose philosophical and religious writings remain influential to this day

Roman Empire was a remarkable civilization that dominated the world for over a thousand years It reached its height of glory in 2nd Century CE when it ruled most of Europe North Africa and the Middle East It was famous for its political military cultural and economic achievements such as its law system engineering wonders art and literature However nothing lasts forever The Roman Empire started to decline in the 3rd century CE due to a series of factors that eroded its strength and cohesion Some of the main causes of the fall of the Roman Empire were Barbarian invasion The Roman Empire faced constant attacks from various groups and peoples that lived outside its borders such as the Goths Huns Vandals and Franks These groups often raided and looted the Roman provinces especially in the West Some of them also settled within empire and challenged its authority In 5th Century CE several barbarian leaders such as Alaric Attila and Odoacer sacked Rome and overthrew last Roman emperors in the West Division and cracks in Rome The Roman Empire became too big and diverse to be governed effectively by a single ruler In 285 CE Emperor Diocletian split the empire into two halves the Western Roman Empire and the Eastern Roman Empire Each half had its own emperor capital administration and army This split weakened the unity and solidarity of the empire as the two halves often competed and conflicted with each other The Western Roman Empire was more exposed to barbarian invasions and economic decline while the Eastern Roman Empire survived longer and became known as the Byzantine Empire Introduction of Christianity Christianity emerged as a new religion in the 1st century CE within the Roman Empire It spread quickly among the lower classes and slaves who were attracted by its message of salvation and equality Christianity also faced persecution and hostility from the pagan authorities who saw it as a threat to their traditional gods and values In 313 CE Emperor Constantine issued the Edict of Milan which granted religious tolerance to Christians In 380 CE Emperor Theodosius made Christianity the official religion of the empire This led to a loss of cultural diversity and a rise of religious conflicts within the empire Economic decline The Roman Empire suffered from various economic problems that undermined its prosperity and stability These included inflation taxation corruption unemployment trade disruption urban decay and rural depopulation The empire also relied heavily on slave labor which reduced innovation and productivity The empire also spent a lot of money on maintaining its army and bureaucracy which drained its resources and increased its debts The fall of the Roman Empire had significant consequences for Europe and the world It marked the end of an era of classical civilization and ushered in a period of political fragmentation cultural decline and social unrest It also opened the way for the emergence of new kingdoms and civilizations such as the Franks the Anglo Saxons the Vikings the Arabs and the Turks Some of these groups preserved and adopted elements of Roman culture and law while others introduced new ideas and innovations The fall of the Roman Empire also influenced the development of Christianity which became the dominant religion in Europe and beyond The rise and fall of the Roman Empire is a fascinating and complex story that has inspired many historians writers and artists It is also a lesson that reminds us of the fragility and resilience of human civilization As Edward Gibbon the author of The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire wrote The story of its ruin is simple and obvious and instead of inquiring why the Roman empire was destroyed we should rather be surprised that it had subsisted so long

The Cyrillic alphabet is a writing system developed in the First Bulgarian Empire during the 9th century AD It was developed during the Christianization of the region with the aim of translating the Bible and other religious texts into the Slavic languages spoken there The Cyrillic script is named after Saint Cyril a monk from Thessaloniki who along with his brother Saint Methodius created the Glagolitic alphabet which predates and heavily influenced the Cyrillic alphabet Here are a few key points about the development of the Cyrillic alphabet Inspiration from the Glagolitic alphabet The Cyrillic alphabet was developed from or at least heavily influenced by the Glagolitic alphabet Cyril and Methodius created the Glagolitic alphabet to translate religious texts into Old Church Slavonic which was the Slavic language spoken at the time The Glagolitic alphabet was quite unique though it had some similarities to Greek and Latin Adaptation and Simplification The Cyrillic alphabet was created by the disciples of Cyril and Methodius particularly by Saint Clement of Ohrid and Saint Naum after Cyril and Methodius s death It was likely developed as a more straightforward easier to use alternative to the Glagolitic alphabet It simplified some of the more complex features of the Glagolitic script and included many letters from the Greek alphabet possibly due to the influence of the Byzantine Eastern Roman Empire which was Greek speaking and Christian Spread Across Eastern Europe and Asia The Cyrillic alphabet spread across Eastern Europe and into Asia with the spread of Orthodox Christianity and the influence of Slavic and later Russian political power Today it s used in various forms by many different languages including Russian Bulgarian Serbian Ukrainian Macedonian and many others Modern Adaptations Over the centuries the Cyrillic script has been adapted to suit the needs of various languages This has resulted in numerous versions of the Cyrillic alphabet with each version having a unique assortment of letters In conclusion the Cyrillic alphabet is a writing system that developed in the 9th century AD in the First Bulgarian Empire influenced by the Glagolitic and Greek alphabets and has since been adapted for use by many different languages

Plovdiv in Bulgaria is one of the most beautiful cities you ve probably never heard of Why With more than 3 000 years of wild history and architecture influenced by three different continents there s simply nowhere else like it So here is the brief story of a hidden gem In 342 BC King Philip II of Macedon father of Alexander the Great founded a city in modern day Bulgaria and called it Philippopolis He picked a naturally advantageous site what with seven steep hills just like Rome rising up around the Maritsa River all within view of the Rhodope Mountains to the south and the Balkans to the north There had already been a town in the area since 6 000 BC it was also once ruled by Xerxes of Persia and Plovdiv is still filled with ruins left by the ancient Thracians who lived in it so for so long But it was Philip who established the first truly major city there and settled a mix of Thracians Macedonians and Greeks within it Over the next two thousand years Plovdiv which has had many names was fought over captured sacked and rebuilt several times Thracians Macedonians Persians Romans including Marcus Aurelius Huns Bulgars Byzantines Crusaders Ottomans and Russians have all fought over or found their way to this old and storied city And what has survived is an architectural and cultural delight Plovdiv is scattered with ancient ruins from the tumbled masonry of Thracian and Byzantine walls on Nebet Tepe one of the seven hills known as tepes from Turkish to the Roman theatre one of the most complete in Europe which regularly hosts musical theatrical performances and the great stadium which once held 30 000 spectators Medieval fortifications have survived too such as the Hisar Kapia Gate and as with many Balkan cities Plovdiv has places of worship belonging to Orthodox Christians Catholics Jews Protestants and Muslims The Dzhumaya Mosque built by the Ottomans when they conquered Plovdiv in the 14th century is the oldest mosque in Europe outside of Iberia Its Old Town which stands on ancient and Medieval foundations was further developed in the mid 19th century during the Bulgarian National Revival as national consciousness awakened and the desire for independence from the Ottomans grew ever stronger hence its profusion of traditional architecture Those timber framed houses with their jettied stories and projecting windows are typical of Medieval Bulgarian architecture And the result is a labyrinth of brightly painted houses and churches built along the cobbled lanes of a Medieval street plan all raised several hundred feet above the surrounding landscape on the three hills of Nebet Tepe Dzhambaz Tepe and Taksim Tepe The city was blessed with a new wave of architecture in the late 19th and early 20th centuries when Bulgaria had revolted from the Ottomans and become an independent kingdom Then influenced by the Central European architecture of the Austro Hungarian Empire Plovdiv s streets were filled with the colourful stucco and eclectic historicism of cities like Vienna Soon enough a neighbourhood called Kapana emerged the cultural and artistic heart of Plovdiv which to this day is filled with artisans workshops galleries caf s and exhibition spaces After that came the USSR and a host of Communist era edifices In other words this city has become an architectural palimpsest of the highest order Plovdiv is an aesthetic delight a city of colour and shape of narrow alleys and shimmering squares of temples and fortresses and of a vibrant living culture And it is also a prime example of architecture s power to tell the whole story of a city Each street is lined with thousands of years of war religion politics cultural exchange revolution technological progress and artistic evolution This is one of the reasons why architecture is so important it s like a language which brings the world to life The buildings of Plovdiv are a physical story waiting to be read Plovdiv s Old Town also speaks to the profound cultural significance of architecture Those traditional houses were about a reawakening of Bulgarian identity after five centuries of enforced sleep under Ottoman rule And this if anything is architecture s greatest significance that the way things are built and how they look matters to people that in buildings can be manifest identity meaning place and purpose Plovdiv is a beautiful city partly because of the unpredictable twists and turns of its history caught as it was between the cultural and geopolitical cross winds of countless different empires and peoples down the centuries and partly by intention because of how the people who live there have chosen to build and design their wonderful city

Around 2000 years ago Roman Empire was not only dominating vast territories on land but was also achieving what to many seemed impossible engineering feats beneath the surface of the sea Without oxygen tanks modern wetsuits or high tech diving gear the Romans designed and built underwater structures that would challenge even 21st Century architects From harbors constructed directly on the sea floor to experimental diving methods their ingenuity continues to astound scholars and engineers alike This little known chapter of Roman innovation reveals a civilization that was not only mastering roads aqueducts and monumental architecture but also the depths of the ocean itself The idea of underwater exploration in the ancient world conjures images of brave mariners and mysterious wrecks but the Romans took it a step further they developed rudimentary diving technologies to stay submerged for extended periods Historical accounts notably from Pliny the Elder and later Byzantine sources refer to urinatores professional divers employed in both military and civilian roles These divers salvaged sunken cargo explored wreckage and assisted in underwater construction But how did they breathe The simplest technique involved using hollow reed tubes extending from the diver s mouth to the surface While this method limited movement and depth due to pressure constraints it allowed them to stay submerged just long enough for short tasks For deeper or more complex dives the Romans may have used primitive diving bells air filled metal or clay containers inverted and placed over the head Though rudimentary these devices trapped enough air to allow a diver to descend up to 30m for short periods according to some reconstructions While archaeological remains of these devices are scarce literary and artistic evidence suggests such innovations were indeed part of Roman maritime operations The ability to work underwater however limited was crucial to the Empire s coastal infrastructure One of the most astonishing Roman engineering feats is the artificial harbor at Caesarea Maritima located on the coast of modern day Israel Commissioned by Herod the Great and completed around 10 BCE this massive port demonstrates the Empire s capacity to construct directly into the sea a task that remains challenging for today s builders Using massive concrete blocks molded and poured underwater Roman engineers created breakwaters and seawalls that formed a fully functional harbor These structures were laid atop submerged timber frameworks filled with volcanic ash based hydraulic concrete and lowered into place with stunning precision Divers and support crews had to coordinate these efforts while battling currents and visibility a testament to their training and ingenuity The entire operation at Caesarea required logistical mastery including quarrying materials transporting them by sea and assembling them underwater The port served as a vital naval and commercial hub connecting Judaea to the broader Roman trade network Despite centuries of erosion parts of the harbor remain intact preserved in part by the remarkable properties of Roman concrete Perhaps the single most significant Roman innovation that made these feats possible was their hydraulic concrete known today as opus caementicium While modern Portland cement crumbles in saltwater over time Roman marine concrete has proven to be incredibly durable even strengthening as it ages The secret lay in its unique composition a blend of lime calcium oxide volcanic ash pozzolana and rubble or gravel When mixed with seawater this combination triggered a chemical reaction that produced calcium aluminum silicate hydrates creating a rock like bond This allowed the concrete to set underwater hardening quickly and bonding with the surrounding materials including natural rock copyright The Archaeologist

Revisiting Historical Narratives Separating Fact from Fiction in the Israeli Palestinian Conflict The Israeli Palestinian conflict deeply rooted in millennia of history is often viewed through the lens of 20th century political developments However understanding this complex conflict requires a much deeper excavation into the historical interactions between Arabs and Jews dating back to ancient times This comprehensive analysis will explore the demographic and cultural presence in the region from the 7th century to the modern era drawing on a wealth of historical knowledge to present a nuanced narrative The Early Islamic Era 7th Century Onwards The 7th century saw significant transformations in the Middle East with the rise of Islam under the leadership of the Prophet Muhammad After Muhammad s death his successors the Caliphs expanded their territory rapidly The Arab Muslim forces conquered the Byzantine province of Palaestina in a series of decisive battles marking the introduction of Islam and initiating the gradual arabization of the region This period was marked by the establishment of Muslim dominance but allowed for religious pluralism under Islamic rule Jewish communities which had been present in the region since ancient times continued to exist in towns such as Jerusalem Tiberias Ramleh Ashkelon Caesarea and Gaza These communities were classified as dhimmis non Muslims living under Muslim governance granted certain protections and subject to specific restrictions This status allowed Jewish communities certain autonomy to manage their civil affairs maintain religious practices and participate in trade and agriculture albeit within a framework that positioned them as subjects with limited political rights The Crusades to Ottoman Rule 11th 16th Century The Crusader period began with the capture of Jerusalem by the Latin Christians in 1099 establishing a series of crusader states that disrupted the lives of both Muslim and Jewish residents The Jewish communities faced massacres and expulsions as the crusaders sought to diminish Muslim and Jewish influence in the Holy Land After nearly two centuries of conflict the region came under the control of the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt which restored a greater degree of stability but continued to maintain the dhimmi system The Mamluk rule was eventually succeeded by the Ottoman Turks who took control in 1517 The Ottoman period is characterized by administrative reorganization and relative religious tolerance Under Ottoman administration the Jewish population remained modest but significant especially in spiritual and cultural centers like Jerusalem Hebron and Safed The Ottomans implemented the millet system which allowed religious minorities considerable autonomy to govern themselves under their own laws and leaders promoting a revival in Jewish religious and communal life The Ottoman Empire and the Modern Era 16th Century 20th Century During the Ottoman reign Palestine was administratively part of the Damascus Eyalet and later the Jerusalem Sanjak The Jewish population experienced growth due to the migration of Sephardic Jews fleeing the Spanish Inquisition who brought with them advanced knowledge of trade and crafts revitalizing the Jewish communities in Palestine The 19th century saw an increased European interest in the region culminating in more significant Jewish immigration influenced by the nascent Zionist movement and escalating antisemitism in Europe This immigration laid the groundwork for the later political developments in Zionism and increased tensions with the Arab population who began to see the rising number of Jewish settlers as a threat to their homeland British Mandate and the Rise of Nationalism 20th Century Following World War I the defeat of the Ottoman Empire led to the British Mandate in Palestine authorized by the League of Nations This period witnessed substantial Jewish immigration facilitated by the British under the terms of the Balfour Declaration which promised the establishment of a Jewish national home in Palestine This influx exacerbated tensions with the Arab population leading to periodic violence and uprisings The conflicting promises made to Arabs in the McMahon Hussein correspondence and to Jews in the Balfour Declaration deepened the divisions setting the stage for the later conflict UN Partition and the Establishment of Israel 1947 1948 The proposal of the UN Partition Plan in 1947 aimed to address the conflict by creating independent Arab and Jewish states This plan was met with mixed reactions the Jewish leadership accepted it as a pragmatic step toward statehood while the Arab leadership rejected it viewing it as further encroachment on their rights and lands The subsequent Arab Israeli War of 1948 resulted in the establishment of Israel and led to significant Palestinian displacement events that have had lasting impacts on the regional dynamics and continue to influence geopolitical relations today The Six Day War and Territorial Changes 1967 In 1967 tensions escalated into the Six Day War wherein Israel achieved a rapid victory and significantly expanded its territory by capturing the West Bank Gaza Strip and East Jerusalem This expansion marked the beginning of the prolonged Israeli occupation of Palestinian territories central to the ongoing conflict The war reshaped the geopolitical landscape and set the stage for future negotiations and conflicts over these territories The Oslo Accords and the Road to Peace 1990s The Oslo Accords represented a landmark in attempts to resolve the conflict initiated in the early 1990s These agreements established the Palestinian Authority and created a framework for potential peace through the creation of autonomous Palestinian zones and the promise of future negotiations aimed at addressing more permanent status issues including borders the status of Jerusalem and the right of return for refugees However the accords faltered in achieving lasting peace primarily due to unresolved core issues and mutual suspicions The Second Intifada to the Present 2000s Onwards The breakdown in peace efforts at the end of the 1990s led to the eruption of the Second Intifada a significant and violent uprising that resulted in a substantial death toll and deepened animosity on both sides This period of intense conflict further strained relations and stalled any progress toward a lasting peace agreement The years following the Intifada have seen continued negotiations but also persistent conflict influenced by internal political dynamics within both Israeli and Palestinian societies as well as broader international geopolitical shifts The landscape of the conflict today remains fraught with recurring tensions and periodic escalations reflecting the enduring complexity and deeply entrenched nature of the conflict Conclusion Understanding the Israeli Palestinian conflict requires recognizing the deep historical roots and complexities that define it A thorough examination of the narrative from ancient times through various empires to the modern era reveals the multifaceted identity of the region Both Jewish and Arab populations have had profound historical ties to this land which complicate the simplistic narratives often presented Only through a comprehensive understanding of this shared history can there be progress towards a lasting peace This exploration aims to provide a foundation for understanding and addressing the narratives that
