The Fall of Rome A Turning Point in History In the annals of history few dates stand as emblematic as September 4 476 AD This year witnessed the symbolic end of the mighty Western Roman Empire when a young emperor named Romulus Augustulus was deposed by Odoacer a Germanic chieftain The city that once stood as a beacon of power and civilization controlling vast territories from Britain to Africa found itself facing its decline But what led to this moment Over time the Western Roman Empire had been beleaguered by internal strife economic difficulties and external pressures from barbarian groups Despite efforts to reinforce its borders and maintain its territorial integrity the empire struggled to adapt to the changing geopolitical dynamics The East and West had been effectively operating as separate entities for years with the Eastern Empire soon to be known as the Byzantine Empire generally faring better in terms of stability and prosperity Odoacer s act in 476 wasn t the first time Rome had been sacked the Visigoths and Vandals had done so in the 5th century But this event was different It wasn t merely a raid or a temporary occupation It signified the end of the line for Roman emperors in the West Odoacer didn t declare himself emperor but rather took the title King of Italy highlighting a shift from the Roman tradition Interestingly the Eastern Roman Empire with its capital in Constantinople would continue to thrive for almost another thousand years as the Byzantine Empire It carried forward the Roman legacy in many ways blending it with Greek and Christian traditions In retrospect the fall of Rome in 476 AD stands not just as an end but as a transition The Early Middle Ages were dawning and Europe s cultural political and social landscapes were set to transform dramatically The legacy of Rome however would echo throughout history its impact undiminished by the passage of time

Source GROK The Monastery of the Mother of God in Hvosno also known as the Holy Virgin of Hvosno or Bogorodica Hvostanska Serbian Albanian Manastiri i Virgj resh s s Shenjt t Hvosnos is a historically significant Serbian Orthodox Christian site located in the village of Vrela also Vrell near Studenica approximately 20 kilometers north of Pe in the historical region of Hvosno within modern Kosovo The monastery dedicated to the Dormition of the Theotokos is currently in ruins but its historical religious and cultural importance endures particularly as a former cathedral seat of the Serbian Orthodox Eparchy of Hvosno Historical Significance Origins and Founding The site s origins trace to the mid 6th century during the early Byzantine period when a three nave basilica with a narthex was constructed within a fortified castrum likely under Emperor Justinian I reflecting early Eastern Roman architectural styles In the third decade of the 13th century c 1220s a new single nave church with a dome and a semi circular apse rectangular externally was erected on the foundations of this earlier basilica commissioned to serve as the cathedral seat of the newly established Serbian Orthodox Eparchy of Hvosno following the creation of the autocephalous Serbian Archbishopric of i a in 1219 under Saint Sava A primary source a Serbian medieval genealogy records Saint Sava appointing the sixth bishop in Hvosno in Mala Studenica in the Church of the Holy Mother of God Medieval Importance The monastery became a central religious institution when the Eparchy of Hvosno was elevated to a Metropolitanate after the Serbian Patriarchate of Pe was established in 1346 under Stefan Du an who incorporated the Hvosno region into his empire It is mentioned in sources from 1473 1566 and 1635 with Metropolitan Victor noted as the last bishop in 1635 The monastery flourished in the 16th century particularly under Monk Makarije later Patriarch Makarije Sokolovi who led artistic and spiritual activities including the writing of a Prologue in 1560 Decline and Abandonment The monastery was abandoned during the Great Serbian Migration of 1690 led by Patriarch Arsenije III amid Ottoman reprisals following the Austro Turkish War 1683 1699 Local Albanians in Vrela reportedly used the monastery s stones for construction including a village mosque accelerating its decay By the 19th century travelers described it as entirely in ruins Religious and Cultural Significance As the seat of the Eparchy of Hvosno the monastery held profound religious importance within the Serbian Orthodox Church symbolizing the integration of spiritual and administrative authority in medieval Serbia It was declared a Monument of Culture of Exceptional Importance by the Republic of Serbia in 1967 and is protected under Kosovo s Law on Special Protective Zones established in 2008 as part of the Ahtisaari Plan which designates a surrounding area to prevent incompatible development and preserve its heritage Culturally it reflects the Byzantine Romanesque ecclesiastical traditions prevalent in the Balkans contributing to the understanding of medieval Serbian art and architecture Although not part of the UNESCO listed Medieval Monuments in Kosovo its historical ties to the Patriarchate of Pe underscore its role in the broader Orthodox heritage of the region Current Status and Recent Events Today the monastery exists primarily as archaeological ruins with foundations and debris visible but the structures largely leveled to the ground It is enclosed by protective wiring and remains under the jurisdiction of the Serbian Orthodox Diocese of Ra ka and Prizren

The Golden Gate of Constantinople constructed during the 4th and 5th centuries CE was a magnificent triumphal arch and the grand ceremonial entrance to the city Located within the Theodosian Walls it symbolized the glory of the Byzantine Empire and was a focal point for imperial processions victories and celebrations Symbolism and Early Grandeur Originally the gate was a monument of splendor wide enough to allow chariots drawn by four elephants to pass through It was built of white marble and adorned with intricate reliefs and gilded statues earning it the name Golden Gate The gate served as a powerful symbol of imperial power marking the entrance to the most important city of the Roman and Byzantine Empires Emperors returning from victorious campaigns entered Constantinople through the Golden Gate greeted by cheering crowds and elaborate ceremonies Shrinking for Defense As the centuries passed and the empire faced increasing threats defense took precedence over aesthetic grandeur The once wide gate was gradually narrowed and fortified to improve its defensive capabilities Towers were added and the passage became less ceremonial and more practical for military use By the Middle Ages the gate was incorporated into a larger defensive complex and its symbolic role faded as Constantinople struggled to withstand sieges and invasions Legacy Though its grandeur has diminished the Golden Gate remains a poignant reminder of the city s former glory Today its remnants can still be seen within modern Istanbul a testament to Constantinople s enduring legacy as the Queen of Cities and the heart of the Byzantine Empire

September 8 1331 Stefan Du an declared himself king of Serbia Stefan Du an one of the most powerful and ambitious rulers in Serbian history declared himself king of Serbia in 1331 marking a pivotal moment in the rise of the Serbian state Du an s reign which would later culminate in his elevation to Emperor of the Serbs and Greeks was characterized by territorial expansion legal reform and a vision of uniting the Balkans under Serbian leadership His declaration as king was both a personal triumph and a significant milestone for the Serbian medieval kingdom setting the stage for its transformation into a regional power Stefan Du an was born around 1308 into the royal Nemanji dynasty which had ruled Serbia for several generations His father King Stefan De anski was a strong ruler who had consolidated Serbian power after the chaotic period of political instability However the relationship between Du an and his father grew strained as Du an matured into a capable military leader By the time Du an reached his early twenties tensions between father and son had reached a breaking point largely due to disagreements over governance and strategy In 1331 Du an led a coup against his father which culminated in the latter s overthrow and imprisonment Stefan De anski was later strangled to death clearing the way for Du an to ascend the throne Though this act of patricide was controversial it was not entirely unusual for the time given the political environment of medieval Serbia and the Balkans where dynastic struggles and violent power transitions were common Du an s seizure of the throne was a pragmatic move designed to ensure his control over the kingdom and to implement his expansive ambitions Upon becoming king Du an immediately set out to expand Serbian territory and influence He led successful military campaigns against neighboring Byzantine territories taking advantage of the internal weakness of the Byzantine Empire which was embroiled in civil wars and political instability By conquering large swaths of Byzantine land including parts of Macedonia Thessaly and Epirus Du an established Serbia as a dominant power in the region His reign marked the height of the Serbian medieval state as he doubled its territory effectively creating a Serbian empire in the Balkans As king Du an was not only a conqueror but also a legislator He introduced a comprehensive legal code known as Du an s Code in 1349 which would become one of the most significant medieval legal documents in the Balkans The code covered a wide range of legal matters including criminal law property law and ecclesiastical law Du an sought to strengthen central authority and unify his realm under a single set of laws which applied to both the Serbian nobility and the church His legal reforms helped to modernize the Serbian state and provided a framework for governance that outlived his reign In 1346 after years of successful conquests and growing power Du an took the extraordinary step of declaring himself Emperor of the Serbs and Greeks This bold move was a clear challenge to the authority of the Byzantine emperor and marked Du an s ambition to supplant the Byzantine Empire as the dominant power in the Orthodox Christian world Du an was crowned in Skopje and the Serbian Orthodox Church was elevated to the status of a patriarchate further solidifying his imperial claim His coronation as emperor was an assertion of both political and religious authority aiming to position Serbia as the new center of Orthodox Christianity The reign of Stefan Du an also marked the zenith of Serbian influence in the Balkans His empire stretched from the Adriatic Sea to the Aegean encompassing much of the territory of modern day Serbia Montenegro North Macedonia Albania and parts of Greece and Bulgaria Du an s ambitions extended beyond mere territorial conquest he sought to create a centralized and powerful state that could rival the Byzantine Empire in both military and cultural terms He encouraged the development of arts and culture and his court in Skopje became a center of learning and religious devotion Despite his achievements Du an s empire was not to last His sudden death in 1355 at the age of 47 left a power vacuum that his son and successor Stefan Uro V was unable to fill The empire quickly began to fracture as internal conflicts and external pressures from the Ottoman Turks and neighboring powers eroded the unity Du an had worked so hard to create Within a few decades of Du an s death the Serbian Empire had effectively disintegrated and the rise of the Ottoman Empire would soon overwhelm the remnants of Serbian independence Nevertheless Stefan Du an s legacy endured He is remembered as one of Serbia s greatest rulers and his reign is often viewed as a golden age in Serbian history His military conquests legal reforms and ambitious vision for a united Balkan empire left a lasting imprint on the region His legal code in particular influenced the development of law in the Balkans for centuries Though his empire did not survive long after his death Du an s declaration as king in 1331 was a turning point that set Serbia on a path Bulgarian history In the spring of 811 in response to Bulgarian campaigns against Serdica and along the Struma River valley the Byzantine emperor Basileus Nikephoros I Genikos organized an army of 25k men for a campaign aimed at the heart of the Bulgarian lands the capital Pliska The Byzantines marched along the coastal road through Mesembria modern Nesebar and after rejecting Khan Krum s offer of peace they crossed the Balkan Mountains Stara Planina in early July defeating the main Bulgarian force about 12k soldiers south of Pliska Instead of defending the capital with his broken army Krum withdrew his forces to preserve and rebuild them Even before the battle with the Byzantines in June Krum had summoned mercenary detachments from the Slavs and Avars under his control Meanwhile Nikephoros seized Pliska and allowed his troops to plunder the city The emperor looted the state treasury and ravaged the area around Pliska delivering a severe blow to the Bulgarian economy Civilian casualties among the Bulgarian population were significant Combined with military losses this weakened the Bulgarians as a dominant ethnic group and prompted future reforms by Krum and his successor Omurtag After several days of pillaging the region around present day Shumen and Targovishte Nikephoros received reports of a concentration of new Bulgarian forces Realizing the threat to his communication lines the emperor ordered a withdrawal through the Balkan Mountains Historians still debate whether the retreat was through the Varbitsa or Rish Pass but this does not significantly affect the course of the campaign Krum had wisely deployed scouts across the Eastern Balkans to monitor Byzantine movements Reinforced by Avar and Slavic mercenaries the Bulgarian army grew to around 8 000 9 000 men Krum divided them into mobile units which he concealed in the mountains On the night of July 25 26 the Byzantine forces were stretched thin within the mountain pass Given their numbers at least 22 k the marching column likely stretched over 10 kilometers and may have included multiple camps The main cavalry occupied the vanguard in the southern part of the pass the imperial elite troops and part of the baggage train were in the center and the remainder of the army was positioned to the north This gave Krum the opportunity to concentrate his forces for a swift strike against the emperor s position In the pre dawn darkness of July 26 the forest around the imperial camp began speaking in Bulgarian The attack was sudden and ruthless The imperial elite fought with desperate determination but were overwhelmed The emperor was killed and his head was presented to Krum Other Bulgarian detachments attacked the Byzantine cavalry throwing them into a panicked retreat Finally the rear part of the Byzantine army was struck and scattered The baggage train and the imperial treasury fell into Bulgarian hands Most of the Byzantine army was either destroyed or captured The defeat was catastrophic Nikephoros Genikos remains one of the few Byzantine emperors to fall in battle This victory allowed Krum to regroup and launch a new offensive against the Byzantines in 812 An Arab engineer who had defected to the Bulgarians along with other Byzantine renegades helped form an engineering corps which enabled the Bulgarians to capture fortresses in the Bay of Burgas The victory at Varbitsa Pass is one of the greatest successes in Bulgarian military history It saved the First Bulgarian Empire which had been pushed to the brink of survival after the destruction of its capital The cool headedness and determination shown by Krum in this dire situation leave no doubt that he is among Bulgaria s greatest rulers

marriages between Georgian rulers and Armenian noble families Marriage to David IV of Georgia Rusudan is traditionally identified as the first wife of King David IV the Builder of Georgia The marriage influential Armenian noble circles Although contemporary Georgian sources do not identify David s first wife by name Armenian historical tradition associates her with the Artsruni dynasty Mother of the Armenian chroniclers the medieval Georgian royal chronicles do not identify David IV s first wife by name or ethnicity Historians have proposed several possible explanations for this omission One alliances As the kingdom s political priorities evolved earlier dynastic connections with the displaced Armenian aristocracy may simply have received less attention in official historiography More broadly medieval chronicles were often selective works composed to advance dynastic religious or political objectives Their silence regarding Rusudan therefore cannot by itself be taken as evidence against her existence or Armenian origin Historical Significance If the traditional identification is correct Rusudan occupies an important place in the shared history of Armenia and Georgia She Charlemagne s Throne located in Aachen Cathedral Germany stands as a profound symbol of medieval European power and the legacy of the Holy Roman Empire This ancient seat of authority not only witnessed the coronation of thirty one German kings but also served as a testament to the cultural and religious aspirations of the time Charlemagne or Charles the Great 742 814 was a pivotal figure in European history As King of the Franks and Lombards and later crowned the first Holy Roman Emperor in 800 AD he played a crucial role in the consolidation of Western Europe His reign marked the Carolingian Renaissance a period of cultural revival characterized by the promotion of learning arts and architecture Aachen located in present day Germany became the center of Charlemagne s empire and his preferred royal residence The city strategically positioned at the crossroads of Europe was chosen for its hot springs and favorable climate It was here that Charlemagne constructed his Palatine Chapel now part of Aachen Cathedral which became the heart of his imperial capital Charlemagne s Throne was not just a symbol of his reign but also a central element in the coronation ceremonies of his successors From early 9th Century until 1531 it served as the coronation throne for thirty one kings of the Germans cementing its place in the annals of European history Throne s use in these ceremonies underscored the continuity and legitimacy of the Holy Roman Empire linking each new ruler to the legacy of Charlemagne The throne itself is an exemplar of early medieval craftsmanship and symbolism It is constructed from simple yet historically significant materials marble slabs believed to have originated from the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem This connection to the Holy Land imbued the throne with a sacred aura reinforcing the divine right of kingship The design of the throne is austere reflecting the early medieval aesthetic and perhaps Charlemagne s own preference for simplicity It consists of a seat made from a solid marble slab supported by four additional stone slabs The throne s backrest is straight and it lacks armrests emphasizing its functional rather than ornamental purpose Charlemagne s Throne is housed within the Palatine Chapel a masterpiece of Carolingian architecture Chapel octagonal in shape features a central domed hall surrounded by a two story ambulatory Its design was inspired by Byzantine architecture of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople and the earlier Roman imperial palaces symbolizing a fusion of Western and Eastern Christian traditions The interior of the chapel is adorned with intricate mosaics marble columns and precious stones reflecting the artistic achievements of the Carolingian Renaissance The throne itself is positioned on an elevated gallery emphasizing its significance and providing a commanding view of the chapel below The use of Charlemagne s Throne for coronations continued until 16th Century Ferdinand I was the last king to be crowned on the throne in 1531 Afterward coronation site moved to Frankfurt Cathedral reflecting changes in the political landscape and the rise of different centers of power within Holy Roman Empire Despite the end of its use as a coronation seat Charlemagne s Throne remains an enduring symbol of medieval kingship and unity of Europe under the Holy Roman Empire Its historical significance and legacy of Charlemagne continue to resonate not only as a relic of a bygone era but also as a symbol of cultural and political continuity Monemvasia is a town and municipality in Laconia Greece The town is located on a island connected to the mainland off the east coast of Peloponnese with a 400 meters long causeway The island is about 300 meters wide and one kilometer long and rises on a plateau about a hundred meters above sea level On the slope of this plateau sea side and hidden from the mainland is a small town This remarkably romantic walled city nestled in the shade of the imposing rock is a veritable living museum of Byzantine Ottoman and Venetian history dating back to 13th Century Monemvasia was built during the 6th century by the inhabitants of ancient Laconia seeking refuge from the Slavic invaders who ruled much of Greece between 500 and 700 AD The rocky islet was separated from the mainland by an earthquake in 375 AD Over the following centuries Monemvasia changed hands several times back and forth between the Venetians and the Turks until the small town was liberated during the Greek War of Independence at the start of the 19th century The name Monemvasia is derived from two Greek words moni and emvasia which means one channel or one pier referring to the narrow causeway which is the only way to enter the city The island was first settled on the top of the plateau which is now referred to as the upper town Gradually the colony spread down the hill and thanks to its unique and well defended position grew into a powerful city During the decline of the Byzantine Empire Monemvasia became its main city and one of the great commercial centers of the Byzantine world and a major trading port with a population of 40 000 In the 18th century Monemvasia began to decline until it was rediscovered by tourists in the 1970s

extraordinary man Islam was very much on the march in Europe during the 8th century conquering virtually all of Spain and was now on the doorstep of the Franks It was only thanks to Martel s brutal victory at the Battle of Tours in 732 that halted the march of the Muslims and saved the Christian west from further assaults Charles Martel was an uncompromising type and he put an end to any tyrannic rule in Frankish territory Charlemagne s father died in 768 and he and his brother Carloman divided the succession between them Carloman didn t last long however and he died just two years later and Charlemagne was elevated to king of the Franks around 770 His first duty was to put a swift end to troublesome areas in his kingdom There was an uprising in Aquitaine which was put down quickly with a combination of diplomacy and a threat of force Then after a difficult progress into Italy via the Alps he put down further trouble in the Lombard region using siege warfare and bringing Italy into line His biggest problem in the early years of his reign as king was putting an end the Frankish war with the Saxons which had dragged on for decades The Saxons had been defeated on countless occasions and brought to terms but any time they were they would almost instantly go back on their word and cause further trouble for the Frankish kings and their people Charlemagne s dealings with the Saxons in Germany continued until the early 9th century when he put an end to the war by splitting up the Saxon tribes and resettled in different regions across his kingdom Charlemagne led various other campaigns where he put down uprisings as swiftly as they had arisen It s worth mentioning here that although Charlemagne was a fantastic military leader it would be easy to assume that family was completely secondary to him but that was not the case As a father he was very close to his children and took them with him on his campaigns Charlemagne avoided marrying off his daughters despite it being custom at the time to do so Whether this was because of his love for his children or for other reasons it can only be speculated His success militarily continued defeating the Huns in a campaign led largely by his son Pepin which proved to be a shrewd decision by the king as the Franks suffered very little damage in the war Charlemagne influence was widespread Constantinople s empire saw itself as Rome not a sequel The Eastern Roman Empire is often placed in a separate category under the later name Byzantine Empire The discussion disputes that framing the state continued to call itself Roman and its subjects remained Roman citizens until Constantinople fell That is more than a dispute over vocabulary A label can turn a long transformation into an apparent rupture If the Eastern Empire is treated as something entirely different the continuity of Roman law citizenship political ideas and institutions becomes harder to see The continuity claim does not require pretending that nothing changed The empire s center shifted to Constantinople its culture evolved and its political environment changed over many centuries The point is that these changes were understood as developments within a Roman state rather than the founding of a successor state The discussion also presents this Roman polity as more complicated than a simple military dictatorship It combined an emperor s concentrated executive and military authority with a republican ideal of acting for the public state Its durability was linked to institutions such as taxation and law not only to force This produces a less tidy but more revealing picture of imperial history identity can persist through profound institutional and cultural change The Eastern Empire was transformed but transformation alone did not erase its Roman political lineage When the people and institutions of a state preserve its identity how much weight should later historical terminology carry

The importance of mercenaries in medieval warfare Mercenaries are viewed very negatively today but this was not always the case in the past In medieval and early modern Europe they were an essential part of warfare and in many cases highly respected To understand why they were so important we must understand the specific political and social conditions in Europe at the time as well as the manner in which wars were fought Medieval Europe was very decentralized and its various kingdoms and rulers simply didn t have the means to train and maintain professional standing armies Armies were organized on a campaign to campaign basis Whenever the need arose soldiers were recruited for a specific campaign and eventually the army was disbanded when the campaign was over or when money ran out The medieval West was dominated by a warrior class of nobility which was trained in the use of arms and also possessed expensive war horses and quality weapons and armor But nobles were not enough for large scale warfare and armies had to be complimented by other troops The main problem here was that warfare was very elitist at the time in the sense that troops needed to be very skilled in order to be effective and proficient on the battlefield Weapons like swords bows javelins crossbows and pole weapons were hard to master and required great skills Being an elite heavy cavalryman lancer like medieval knights or for example a proficient horse archer required a lifetime of training Equipment and weapons were also expensive That meant that the number of skilled quality warriors in Europe was actually quite small Let s go through the kind of environments that could provide best warriors in medieval Europe and which troops in particular achieved great renown as mercenaries Besides the nobility the best trained troops were usually urban militias Population of medieval cities was very warlike and took pride in their militias Combat guilds were established where training was provided for citizens Wealthy merchants who could afford good armor also served in such militias Italian city states had good militias especially the maritime republics which had to maintain a certain number of skilled crossbowmen on their galleys The best known example of this are the Genoese crossbowmen Good urban militias also existed elsewhere Flemish militias proved their worth against French knights and won the Battle of the Golden Spurs in 1302 Pope Pius II commented in 1444 how skilled urban militias were in the Holy Roman Empire Not only every noble but even every burgher in the guilds has an armoury in his house so as to appear equipped at every alarm The skill of the citizens in the use of weapons is extraordinary A 15th century depiction of the Genoese mercenaries at the Battle of Cr cy in 1346 There were also some rural commoners who would develop very good fighting skills in some circumstances These were usually people from a landowning yeoman class a middle class between nobility and serfs These were men who could afford better weapons and become good at them The famed English longbowmen are a perfect example of that You also had cases of serfs rising through social ranks through fighting skills and becoming a special warrior class like the ministeriales knights in the Holy Roman Empire These ministeriales entered military service of their lords and often performed administrative functions such as managing castles Eventually they became a warrior class of its own and part of lower nobility They evolved into Imperial knights and served the Emperor directly becoming an essential part of Imperial army A specific type of environment which produced great warriors were various borderlands which experienced frequent fighting and raiding and where people needed to develop martial skills to survive This often happened on the borders of Latin Christendom such as Iberia the Balkans and the Baltics The almogavars from the Crown of Aragon are a good example of that as well as various types of light cavalry from the wars with the Ottomans such as the stradioti and the hussars Another case of fierce borderland warriors were the border reivers on the Anglo Scottish border There were also certain parts of Europe where common people had more freedom and therefore more incentives to fight in wars and defend it such as the Swiss or the Frisians But most common people in the Middle Ages would not make good soldiers and generally had no desire to fight in wars either This was an age before modern nationalism and people would not identify with their country in the same way modern people would Other than religion there was no ideology that could mobilize a large number of people to fight People served specific lords and generally not much would change if some other noblemen took their place Most people simply didn t have a stake in various dynastic conflicts between nobility other that they wanted these conflicts to end as soon as possible as they did not want their lands raided The rare exceptions where you might see some patriotic spirit were the city republics and specific forms of state like the Old Swiss Confederacy Such states might sometimes develop a more warlike spirit among population and train their citizens in organized guilds but were also constrained by their small size Another factor was that even many well trained troops had little motivation to fight on campaigns far away from home While urban militias could perform well when they had to defend their cities sending them on campaigns to some distant lands was a different matter Using unskilled and badly motivated peasant levies was therefore a last resort and used only to compliment the existing elite armies not something a ruler would want to base his army on for a prolonged campaign So if you put all of this together you can see why mercenaries became so important The pool of trained warriors who were eager to fight in wars was simply very small in medieval Europe but demand was often high as wars broke out quite often including prolonged conflicts that spanned over decades People who were trained in the art of war and were veterans of various conflicts became highly sought after as mercenaries and could earn a lot of money by fighting all over the continent for whoever would pay them as well as climb the social ranks this way The story of John Hawkwood the 14th century English mercenary and veteran of the Hundred Years War who ended up fighting in Italy for various lords is probably the best example of that He led the mercenary White Company and made a lot of money fighting in many Italian conflicts He came from humble origins but achieved great fame and wealth as a soldier of fortune John Hawkwood at the Battle of Castagnaro in 1387 He achieved many great victories as the leader of the mercenary White Company and earned a lot of wealth serving various Italian states Medieval mercenaries came from the ranks of the various elite and trained units from all over Europe that I described previously There were many knights from the ranks of nobility who served as mercenaries in conflicts in other lands They were trained as warriors and serving as mercenaries was a great way for them to use their skills to earn some money This was an especially great incentive for impoverished knights There were also many specific units that earned great reputation as mercenaries due to mastering a specific style of fighting that the major powers were deficient in The Genoese crossbowmen were hired by France which lacked quality archers to deal with English longbowmen During the wars against the Cathars in 13th century the French hired experienced Basque mountaineers to help them conquer the Cathar fortresses which were on top of mountains and hard to reach The English longbowmen who were veterans from the Hundred Years War ended up serving in Italy Later on the Swiss pikemen would be highly sought after for their specific style of infantry fighting Hussites also became highly valuable mercenaries because of their experience with handguns and war wagons Various light cavalry troops from the Balkans gave versatility to Western armies that were used to rely only on heavy cavalry The use of such mercenaries meant that medieval armies in Europe were often very multi ethnic consisting of men from various races of Europe and sometimes even with origins from outside of Europe Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II settled Muslim Saracens on Italian mainland and recruited them as soldiers on his campaigns using them as archers and light cavalry Thousands of these Muslims fought in the Imperial army at Cortenuova in 1237 and at Parma in 1248 There was so many of them that the Emperor was mockingly referred to as the Sultan by his enemies Hungarian kings used pagan Cumans who had settled in Hungary as horse archers and light cavalry They contributed to joint Hungarian and Habsburg victory against the Bohemians at the Battle on the Marchfeld in 1278 Likewise Christian knights sometimes served as mercenaries in Muslim armies Henry of Castile the Senator led a contingent of Castilian knights to fight as mercenaries for Muslim emirs in North Africa in 13th century earning a lot of wealth in the process The number of mercenaries kept increasing in next centuries 14th century saw emergence of large mercenary free companies particularly in France and Italy as a result of prolonged wars there These could number thousands of men and were often led by very ambitious and brutal men like Werner von Urslingen a Swabian nobleman who commanded a large mercenary company in Italy or Arnaud de Cervole the Archpriest who served in the Hundred Years War and eventually commanded his own mercenary company as well Besides serving the lords who hired them these men often also plundered and extorted the local population This led to a massive problem as these mercenary companies turned to banditry during peace time Men serving in them often had no intention to return to a peaceful life and wanted to continue to make a living by waging war Marauding bands of unemployed mercenaries became a huge problem in France which saw the rise of so called Tard Venus bands after peace treaty was made with England in 1360 A royal army was sent to deal with them but was defeated The best way to deal with marauding mercenaries was to try to send them to serve in another conflict in another country Bertrand du Guesclin eventually employed a lot of free company mercenaries who were marauding in France for an expedition in Spain where they fought in the Castilian Civil War Being a warrior in the Middle Ages was not just a profession but a way of life Wars gave birth to powerful violent warriors and once these wars ended the rulers recognized that the men who distinguished themselves in war could become a problem during peace time Such was the case with the elite almogavar warriors who served the Crown of Aragon They were elite light infantrymen who originally fought as frontiersmen during the Reconquista but eventually ended up fighting the French Angevins in the War of the Sicilian Vespers After this war ended in 1302 they were organized into the Catalan Company and went to serve the Byzantine Empire King Frederick III of Sicily had no desire to have such violent men in his land in peaceful times as he was aware that they would cause problems The Catalan Company arrives in Constantinople in 1302 The problem of marauding mercenary companies showed the obvious downside of large scale employment of mercenaries In the 15th century the Kingdom of France tried to solve this problem by attempting to form their own infantry of franc archers free archers recruited from the strongest and most capable peasants who were exempt from certain obligations in exchange for being part of a regular infantry force and trained in both archery and melee weapons But this attempt of creating a standing army did not achieve the desired success While the franc archers could be useful for defending their land against bandits and as frontier troops to protect the borderlands their effectiveness on military campaigns in foreign lands proved to be very bad and they were not on the level of elite mercenaries Such was the case in French campaigns in Flanders and Italy in late 15th century where the franc archers performed poorly They were prone to desertion and capitulation once again reflecting the main problem of levied infantries which was that they were simply not motivated to fight for causes that did not involve defending their own land This is why the French ultimately preferred to rely on the elite Swiss mercenaries as their infantry for their aggressive campaigns in other countries Swiss mercenaries also called the Reisl ufer rose to fame in 15th century as the Swiss achieved numerous impressive victories fighting for the Old Swiss Confederacy against external enemies They pioneered infantry tactics with long pikes and halberds which proved to be very effective They also became renowned for their warlike spirit and ruthless approach to war not taking any prisoners Another advantage was their military organization and recruitment The Old Swiss Confederacy was organized into cantons which had their own militias The Swiss mercenaries could be hired from Swiss cantons as a ready made army of local soldiers who spoke the same language and knew each other making them more reliable in battles This also meant that it was easier for a wealthy power like France to purchase Swiss mercenaries as they only needed to approach the governments of the Swiss cantons rather than deal with the mercenaries directly In return mercenary service became a major source of wealth for the Old Swiss Confederacy and a great way for poor Swiss to earn money Military became a source of great pride for the Swiss and besides money they were also motivated to fight well on campaigns for foreign lords to preserve their reputation as the best warriors in Europe The Swiss pikemen developed a fierce reputation and became highly sought after as mercenaries In late 15th century large elite mercenary armies were employed by the rulers who were able to afford them The mercenary Black Army used by the King of Hungary Matthias Corvinus proved to be extremely successful in the 1470s and the 1480s and enabled him to subdue much of Central Europe while also keeping his kingdom safe from the expanding Ottoman Empire He used Bohemians trained in Hussite war wagon tactics for infantry German knights as heavy cavalry and Serbian hussars for light cavalry This is another example of how elite mercenaries were able to cover deficiencies in European armies making possible more versatile tactics for different types of warfare Relying on heavy cavalry composed of nobility was not enough armies also needed elite infantry and artillery to win wars If there was a shortage of troops trained in particular type of warfare at home rulers looked abroad to hire them as mercenaries But the main problem still remained similar as in the previous centuries Despite the growing European states having increased capacity to hire large number of mercenaries the number of elite mercenary units that were available over Europe was still limited Swiss pikemen were highly sought but were also expensive and there was only so many of them Furthermore the Swiss refused to fight if fellow Swiss were present in the opposite army Such was the case at Novara in 1500 when both France and Milan hired the Swiss mercenaries The Swiss in the Milanese service mutinied and left the battle leading to the capture of the Duke of the Swiss This is how the Landsknecht mercenaries were born They imitated the Swiss tactics in which they were trained by foreign instructors rising to prominence in late 15th century The Landsknechts for influence in Italy and they all hired either the Swiss or the Landsknechts at some point The Swiss were even hired by the Pope in 1506 to serve as his guard which still exists to this day This increased need for mercenaries also popularized the mercenary lifestyle The Landsknechts evolved into a specific social group in the Holy Roman Empire and their lifestyle became attractive to a number of adventurous men Among mercenaries you could find men from all social classes There were nobles and burghers from reputed families But most were from poorer backgrounds Many were outcasts men with followers often exceeded the number of actual soldiers These camp followers provided various services and created a social environment for mercenary soldiers while they were detached from regular settled society Mercenaries could travel with their families or concubines They had their own rules and created a sort of parallel society The Landsknecht mercenaries became famous for their distinct ostentatious fashion as Emperor Maximilian made them exempt from sumptuary laws allowing them to wear what they wanted This lifestyle became very attractive to men who wanted to get away from regular was traditionally centered around warrior culture and raiding Conquest of Italy In 568 AD Alboin led the Lombards alongside other Germanic tribes in a large scale invasion of Italy The Lombards seeking new lands to settle overwhelmed the weakened Byzantine Empire s defenses and swiftly conquered much of northern Italy Alboin s leadership and military prowess played a crucial role in the Lombard conquest of Italy Under his command the Lombards established a kingdom that would endure for centuries becoming known as the Lombard Kingdom or Lombard Italy Ruling Lombard Italy After the conquest Alboin assumed the title of king and established his capital in Pavia He implemented a system of land distribution among his followers rewarding them with estates seized from the local Roman aristocracy Alboin s reign was marked by both consolidation and conflict He faced resistance from the Byzantine Empire as well as from local Italian populations and rival Germanic tribes However he also succeeded in expanding Lombard territory through further military campaigns Death and Legacy Alboin s reign came to a violent end in 572 AD According to historical accounts his wife Rosamund feeling humiliated by Alboin s treatment of her conspired with Alboin s chief cupbearer Peredeo to assassinate him After Alboin s death his kingdom was thrown into turmoil with rival factions vying for power Eventually Alboin s successor Cleph would stabilize Lombard rule in Italy Despite his violent end Alboin s legacy endures in Lombard history as the founder of the Lombard Kingdom in Italy Another view of The underground city of Derinkuyu is an archaeological wonder located in the Cappadocia region of Turkey It is more than 85 meters below the surface of the Earth and consists of an eighteen level tunnel system A local found one of the entrances in 1963 After more thorough investigation and some digging a passage was discovered which was later followed by about six hundred similar discoveries in other private houses Excavations began immediately and traces of an entire civilization were revealed below the surface with residential houses feed storage rooms cattle stables school wine cellars and chapel The first few levels of the cave system were dug out by the Hettites when the Frigians attacked them around 1200 BC most of the city was probably built by the Frigians afterwards The caves could originally be used for storing goods but at the same time they provided a shelter from the current occupiers Each level of the city was carefully planned and divided according to specific goals Each level is closed by a circular rock which can only be moved from the inside with a small perfectly round hole carved in the middle so that the intruders could be measured with a spear They used clay pots as a toilets lived next to torchlight designated a place for dead bodies and animals were kept in the areas closest to the surface to reduce the flow of odors and toxic gases as well as to provide a living insulation layer for the cold months But the most impressive part of the building is the complex ventilation system and the protected well which provided the whole city with fresh air and clean water Thanks to more than fifty ventilation vents air flowed naturally into residential houses and corridors and the more than 55 meters deep well could be closed from underneath to prevent the enemy from access Derinkuyu s exact function remains a topic of discussion It is certain that its construction and use reflects a remarkable social and technical organizational level Discovering is like stepping back in time Walking through the corridors the visitors can experience for themselves what life was like in an underground world which is invisible to the naked eye but very mysterious The secret will capture the imagination of future generations

Khwarizmi a Persian who lived from 780 to 850 He was one of the first to work at the House of Wisdom and thus laid the groundwork for future advances in mathematics Among his greatest contributions was the adoptionof the Indian numeral system and its dissemination Previously the de facto system was based on the ubiquitous Roman numerals which had their limitations Complex math problems involving non integer numbers were near impossible with the Roman system but the Indian system 1 2 3 4 allowed large and negative numbers to be more easily expressed easing complex problems Al Khwarizmi not only borrowed the system from the ancient Indians but also added on to it an important missing link the zero Although he was unable to mathematically prove zero since anything divided by zero is undefined al Khwarizmi implemented it in his further studies revolutionizing some subjects and inventing others Perhaps al Khwarizmi s greatest contribution was the development of algebra In his geography Here al Khwarizmi was a trailblazer While the ancient Greeks were masters of geometry they failed to separate theoretical algebra from it and thus found limitations to the science Al September 4 1282 Peter III of Aragon became the King of Sicily Peter III of Aragon became King of Sicily in 1282 during one of the most dramatic political upheavals of the late 13th century This event marked a critical turning point in Mediterranean geopolitics bringing the Kingdom of Sicily under Aragonese control after a long period of conflict between the papacy the French and the Sicilian populace His ascension to the Sicilian throne was closely tied to the infamous Sicilian Vespers an uprising by the people of Sicily against their Angevin rulers which triggered a broader conflict known as the War of the Sicilian Vespers The roots of Peter III s rise to power in Sicily go back to his marriage to Constance of Sicily the daughter of King Manfred of Sicily who had been defeated and killed by Charles of Anjou in 1266 This marriage gave Peter a legitimate claim to the Sicilian throne although at the time the kingdom was ruled by the French Angevins who had taken control of the island following Manfred s death The Angevins led by Charles of Anjou were unpopular with the Sicilian populace who resented their harsh rule and the heavy taxes imposed on them This discontent eventually exploded into open revolt The Sicilian Vespers which began on March 30 1282 was a violent rebellion that saw thousands of French soldiers and civilians massacred across Sicily The revolt was sparked in Palermo but quickly spread to other parts of the island The Sicilian rebels in need of external support to rid themselves of Angevin rule turned to Peter III of Aragon who had long harbored ambitions to expand his influence in the Mediterranean Peter sailed with a fleet from Tunisia where he had been on a campaign and landed in Sicily where he was welcomed as a liberator He was proclaimed King of Sicily in the city of Palermo on August 30 1282 Peter s acquisition of the Sicilian crown did not go uncontested His claim was immediately challenged by Charles of Anjou who sought to reclaim the island for his dynasty This set the stage for a protracted conflict between the Kingdom of Aragon and the French Angevins with the Papacy also playing a significant role in the dispute Pope Martin IV a staunch supporter of Charles of Anjou excommunicated Peter III and declared a crusade against him urging European rulers to join the effort to depose him Despite the papal opposition and the military efforts of the Angevins Peter III managed to hold onto Sicily thanks to his skillful diplomacy and the support of the Sicilian people He secured alliances with other Mediterranean powers including the Byzantine Empire and utilized the powerful Aragonese fleet to maintain control over the island The War of the Sicilian Vespers would drag on for years with several attempts by the Angevins to retake the island failing Ultimately the war ended in a stalemate and Sicily remained under the control of the Aragonese dynasty Peter III s reign over Sicily marked the beginning of a new era in the island s history His rule and that of his successors tied Sicily more closely to the Aragonese Crown shifting the island s political and cultural orientation towards the western Mediterranean This period also saw Sicily become a key battleground in the broader power struggle between the major European powers of the time particularly the Kingdom of Aragon the Kingdom of France and the Papacy Peter III s conquest of Sicily also had far reaching consequences for the political landscape of Italy and the Mediterranean It weakened the Angevin presence in southern Italy and disrupted the balance of power between the French and Spanish monarchies Furthermore the Aragonese control of Sicily helped to establish a lasting Spanish influence over the island which would continue for centuries ultimately contributing to the creation of the Spanish Empire in the Mediterranean Peter III of Aragon s assumption of the Sicilian throne was not merely a territorial gain it was also a significant assertion of Aragonese power and ambition in the Mediterranean It laid the groundwork for future Aragonese and Spanish expansion in the region influencing the course of European history for generations to come His reign over Sicily although won through violence and war was a testament to his political acumen military skill and ability to capitalize on the discontent of the On October 26 1185 the Uprising of Asen and Peter began sparking a rebellion that would ultimately end Byzantine rule in the Balkan region and lead to the establishment of the Second Bulgarian Empire This revolt led by the brothers Asen and Peter was a fierce response to Byzantine oppression particularly heavy taxation and it set the stage for the re emergence of an independent Bulgarian state after nearly two centuries under Byzantine control The rebellion began in the context of mounting grievances against the Byzantine Empire which had ruled over Bulgaria since 1018 Emperor Isaac II Angelos facing financial difficulties imposed new and burdensome taxes on his subjects including those in the Balkan territories The local population largely Bulgarian and Vlach felt the economic strain deeply as they were already struggling under heavy tax burdens and were denied positions of influence within the Byzantine administration These mounting injustices fueled widespread resentment and gave Asen and Peter a powerful cause around which they could rally support Asen and Peter were local nobles of Bulgarian and Vlach descent who sought to capitalize on this unrest They initially approached Emperor Isaac II with requests for military positions and tax relief for their people However their demands were dismissed and they were reportedly humiliated by the emperor Seizing the opportunity presented by the Byzantine Empire s waning control over its northern territories the brothers returned home and raised the banner of rebellion proclaiming the re establishment of an independent Bulgarian state The timing of the uprising was critical Asen and Peter chose the feast day of St Demetrius a highly revered saint in the region as a symbolic day to launch their revolt According to tradition the brothers claimed to have seen a vision of St Demetrius abandoning Thessalonica symbolizing the saint s support for their cause and the impending downfall of Byzantine authority This spiritual element attracted widespread support among the Bulgarian and Vlach populations who saw the rebellion not only as a fight for independence but also as a divine mission The rebellion spread rapidly across the Balkans as Asen and Peter s forces clashed with Byzantine armies Although initially outnumbered and lacking resources the brothers used guerrilla tactics and the rugged terrain to their advantage steadily wearing down the Byzantine forces Over the course of several years the rebellion gained momentum with Asen and Peter successfully capturing key fortresses and cities solidifying control over large swathes of the Balkan region By 1187 after a series of Byzantine defeats the empire was forced to recognize the independence of the new Bulgarian state establishing the Second Bulgarian Empire with Peter as its first ruler This marked a significant shift in the balance of power in the region as the re established Bulgarian Empire would grow to become a dominant force in southeastern Europe over the next century rivaling both the Byzantine Empire and the Hungarian Kingdom

A Brief History of How Humanity Learned to Eat For most of human history people ate with their hands When Jesus shared meals in first century Judea he ate as everyone around him did using his hands and pieces of bread to scoop up food This wasn t due to a lack of sophistication but simply how people ate Ritual hand washing before meals was an important practice precisely because hands were the primary eating utensils and this made eating with hands arguably more hygienic than it might first appear This hands on approach to eating wasn t unique to the Middle East In ancient India eating with the hands was and remains the traditional method deeply embedded in both practical and philosophical traditions Ayurvedic philosophy teaches that each finger represents one of the five elements and that touching food engages these elements to aid digestion The sensory experience of feeling the temperature and texture of food is considered an important part of the meal Even today many Indians prefer eating with their hands for traditional meals regardless of whether utensils are available The hygienic logic of hand eating is straightforward when you eat with your hands you wash them immediately before the meal You know exactly how clean they are because you ve just cleaned them yourself By contrast utensils like forks and spoons may have been washed hours or days earlier handled by others stored in drawers and touched multiple times before reaching your mouth In cultures where hand eating is traditional the ritual of washing hands before meals isn t casual it s a thorough deliberate practice that ensures cleanliness This explains why hand washing customs were so important in Jewish tradition and why the Gospels mention disputes about proper hand washing techniques Meanwhile on the other side of the world a different eating technology had already taken hold Chopsticks emerged in China over 3 000 years ago during the Shang Dynasty initially as cooking tools for stirring and retrieving food from hot pots By the Han Dynasty 206 BCE 220 CE they had become widespread eating utensils The transition was driven by practical factors population growth and fuel scarcity led people to cut food into smaller pieces that cooked faster making chopsticks more practical than knives at the table Confucian values which discouraged having knives associated with violence at the dining table further encouraged their use From China chopsticks spread to Korea Vietnam and Japan over the following centuries Spoons have an even older history They weren t invented by any particular person or culture but evolved independently across the world as one of humanity s most basic tools Prehistoric peoples fashioned spoon like implements from shells wood and animal horns Ancient Egyptians Greeks and Romans crafted spoons from bronze and silver The spoon s purpose was obvious and universal it was simply the most practical way to eat liquids and soft foods Forks however have a surprisingly recent and contentious history While two pronged forks existed in ancient Greece and Rome they were used only for cooking and serving never for eating The personal dining fork emerged in the Byzantine Empire around the 7th century among the wealthy elite The famous turning point came around 1004 CE when Maria Argyropoulina a Byzantine princess married a Venetian doge and brought golden forks to Venice Venetian society was scandalized Clergy condemned forks as excessive and impious arguing that God had given humans fingers for eating The fork slowly spread through Italy between the 14th and 16th centuries then gradually moved to France and England Even in the 17th century many Europeans still ate primarily with knives and hands viewing forks as effeminate or pretentious It took nearly a millennium for the Byzantine innovation to become standard across Europe FIN

The summer snows of China the crop failures in Ireland and the drought plagued fields of Scandinavia were not the result of divine wrath as chroniclers assumed but of a massive volcanic eruption likely in Iceland that had ejected a blanket of sulfate aerosols into the stratosphere It was the worst year to be alive in the last 2 000 years Yet from this desperate darkness the modern world was born This is the story of how a single environmental catastrophe acting like a stone dropped into a pond sent ripples through history that we are still feeling today It is a story of famine plague and ultimately survival and transformation The immediate impact was agricultural collapse In Europe temperatures dropped by 2 5 degrees Celsius Without sunlight crops failed The Byzantine historian Procopius wrote that the sun gave forth its light without brightness like the moon People were terrified They did not eat the bread of summer but the weeds of the field The famine was so severe that the great city of Constantinople the jewel of the Roman Empire was forced to ration bread But the true cataclysm came in 541 A D when the shockwaves of this climatic shift delivered a second even deadlier blow The weakened population suffering from malnutrition became the perfect host for a new disease From the ports of Egypt rats carrying fleas infected with Yersinia pestis sailed to Constantinople The Plague of Justinian had begun Over the next two centuries this pandemic killed an estimated 50 million people half the population of Europe The Roman Empire already reeling from the climate disaster was broken Its attempts to reunite the Mediterranean under one rule failed not due to barbarian invasions but due to a silent bacterium Here is the counterintuitive twist disaster unlocked human potential With the collapse of the centralized slave dependent Roman system the economic landscape shifted Land was suddenly abundant but laborers were scarce The feudal system that emerged gave peasants negotiating power They demanded better rights fixed rents and freedom from the draconian bondage of the past In the ashes of the empire the seeds of the modern European peasantry and eventually the merchant class were sown Meanwhile in the Arabian Peninsula the chaos in the north left a power vacuum The trade routes that had once enriched the empires of Byzantium and Persia were disrupted It was in this context of economic realignment and spiritual seeking that a merchant named Muhammad began to preach a new message of monotheism in Mecca Within a century the Islamic Caliphates would rise not just as a religious force but as a scientific one The Arabs inheriting the knowledge of Greece and Persia became the librarians of the world preserving mathematics and astronomy while Europe stumbled through the Dark Ages Fast forward to the 14th century The descendants of that same bacterium returned The Black Death ravaged Europe killing a third of its population And once again the same pattern emerged population collapse led to labor shortages which led to higher wages which led to the obsolescence of the feudal system The resulting social mobility funded the Renaissance The terror of death inspired the obsession with life and human potential the very foundation of the Enlightenment and modern science We often view history as a series of wars and political treaties the actions of great men like Caesar or Napoleon But the deeper truth is that we are and always have been at the mercy of the planet The volcanic winter of 536 didn t just ruin a harvest it toppled an empire The Plague didn t just kill millions it liberated the serf The hardship didn t just cause despair

people After Solomon s death the kingdom split into the northern Kingdom of Israel and the southern Kingdom of Judah The northern kingdom fell to the Assyrians in 722 BCE leading to the exile of the ten tribes while the Kingdom of Judah survived until the Babylonian conquest in 586 BCE when Jerusalem was sacked and the First Temple destroyed This exile known as the Babylonian Captivity began a period of diaspora but did not sever the Jewish connection to the land When the Persian Empire allowed Jews to return the Second Temple was rebuilt in Jerusalem around 516 BCE and Jewish religious life resumed under successive Persian Greek and Roman rule Under the Romans tensions between Jewish inhabitants and Roman authorities escalated leading to the Jewish Roman Wars and the destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE The final blow came after the Bar Kokhba Revolt in 135 CE when Emperor Hadrian renamed Judea as Syria Palaestina deliberately attempting to erase Jewish ties to the land associated with an Arab nation state until the 20th century Jewish identity and the connection to the land remained intact through centuries of Byzantine Muslim Crusader Mamluk and Ottoman rule In the late 19th and early 20th centuries Zionism emerged advocating for a Jewish homeland in response to rising European antisemitism Jewish immigration to Ottoman Palestine grew particularly under British control following World War I and the Balfour Declaration of 1917 The British Mandate saw increased Jewish immigration but also rising tensions between Jewish and Arab populations After the Holocaust millennia The modern usage of Palestine as a political identity for Arabs emerged with the founding of the Palestine Liberation Organization PLO in 1964 aimed at reclaiming land from Israel However historically the term had been used by foreign powers and did not represent an Arab nation state before the 20th century Israel on the other hand is the modern expression of a Jewish identity and connection that has endured since ancient times through periods of exile and return In conclusion the Jewish connection to Israel is not a modern construct but the continuation of a deep rooted relationship spanning thousands of years The State of Israel established in 1948 represents the fulfillment of a national dream held by the Jewish people for millennia affirming their enduring presence and sovereignty in the land of their ancestors Despite centuries of foreign rule and efforts to erase their connection the Jewish people never relinquished their ties to their historic A map illustrating the religious landscape of the Arabian Peninsula in the early fifth century Long before the rise of Islam Arabia was far more religiously diverse than it is often portrayed Traditional Arabian polytheism remained dominant across much of the peninsula but Jewish Christian Zoroastrian and other monotheistic traditions had also developed important communities and areas of influence Local pagan beliefs varied between tribes and regions Different communities worshipped their own gods maintained sacred sites and followed distinct rituals rather than belonging to one unified religion Trade routes connected Arabia with the Byzantine and Sasanian empires East Africa and the wider Middle East allowing religious ideas to travel alongside goods and people Christianity became established around parts of northern Arabia the Persian Gulf and the south Jewish communities were especially important in western Arabia and Yemen where Judaism gained political influence within the Himyarite kingdom Zoroastrian influence was strongest in areas connected to the Sasanian Persian Empire particularly around eastern and northeastern Arabia The map also includes Hanifism and Sabianism but these categories are much harder to place geographically The term hanif is associated with individuals who rejected polytheism and worshipped one God without clearly belonging to Judaism or Christianity The identity of the Sabians is also debated with historians linking the name to several different religious communities These borders should therefore be treated as broad areas of influence rather than fixed religious territories Beliefs often overlapped changed through trade and political alliances and varied from one settlement or tribe to another This diverse religious world formed the setting in which Islam emerged in the early seventh century interacting with the pagan Jewish Christian and other traditions already present across Arabia

For people who don t understand what this means here s an abbreviated history lesson What s proscription It was essentially a list made of enemies of the state There were a variety of punishments for different crimes one could be listed for It ranged from death loss of citizenship loss of family rights loss of possessions or all of the above Death was a VERY common punishment and was referred to as summum supplicium or the extreme penalty For treason the punishment was nearly always death So here s a short recap of Marius vs Sulla Marius was a warrior turned Roman politician who was elected 7x to the highest elected office in Rome The 7th time it happened amid division among Rome when he joined forces with Cinna They captured Rome and then both Marius and Cinna were elected consuls This joining of forces is important later Marius is remembered in part for settling his political scores by jailing killing or exiling people that he deemed as enemies of the state via proscriptions One of the people Marius had declared an enemy of the state was Sulla but he escaped death Sulla was another general turned politician who took power through force after he won a civil war Some say he would ve never taken power if Marius hadn t meddled in his military command Marius hated Sulla and the feeling was mutual Marius set the standard of proscriptions being used to settle political scores but he died before Sulla took his revenge Sulla used that standard set by Marius to exact political revenge of his own Marius only son died fighting against Sulla in 82 Sulla wanted to take his revenge against all the former supporters of Marius and Cinna who he felt had wronged him So in 82 BC Sulla instituted the process of proscriptions again to purge the state of former Marius and Cinna supporters Estimates range from 500 to 4 000 Marius Cinna supporters condemned to death Their supporters were named as enemies of the state and anyone who murdered them got to split their property with the state People were given reward money for reporting others who supported him Many were decapitated and had their heads displayed in the Forum or in the streets as a lesson The money the state took from these people helped pay for the endless wars Rome fought Their relatives were punished as well Many say without the earlier proscriptions Sulla would ve never gotten away with this Instead because it was all normalized Sulla ruled and later retired in Roman luxury The lesson is that when you set new rules or standards they often boomerang back you in politics It s best not to create new standards or rules that you don t want to have deployed against your side or your loved ones

II thus the name Theodosian Walls protected city of Constantinople capital of Eastern Roman Empire better known as Byzantine Empire For centuries this imposing structure posed an unsurmountable obstacle to waves of invaders who tried to conquer the city and by extension Empire Finally in 1453 more than a thousand years after their construction Theodosian Walls fell to the fire of Ottoman cannons However Walls outlived both the Roman and Ottoman Empires and still stand in the heart of modern day Istanbul Theodosian Walls are not the first defensive walls of Constantinople Following the foundation and the subsequent dedication of Constantinople on 11 May 330 Emperor Constantine the Great protected his city with new wall However collapse of the Danubian frontier following the Battle of Adrianople in 378 required more formidable defenses to protect the capital of Eastern Roman Empire Finally in early 5th Century emperor Theodosius II commissioned new walls known as Theodosian Walls New defensive perimeter was completed in nick of time preventing Attila Hun and his army from taking the city Attila s Huns were only first of many invaders whose dreams of the conquest of Constantinople were halted by the imposing Theodosian Walls Theodosian Walls when finally completed measured around 12km in length defending the approaches to Constantinople by land The walls consisted of three lines of defense The would be conqueror had first to cross the wide moat filled with water protected by the low wall 1 5m tall Next invader would have to cross open ground before reaching the outer wall 8 9m in height Then if the invader were lucky enough he would have to cross another open space finally reaching the lynchpin of the city s defense massive inner wall 12m high and almost 5m thick Both walls were intersected with towers which held artillery engines Such a system provided the defender with an ideal killing field No wonder for a thousand years no invader managed to take the city Besides their defensive purpose Theodosian Walls presented a powerful and striking symbol of Empire s power to anyone who approached Constantinople by land Imagine the weary traveler who after days weeks or even months reached the imperial capital In most cases he would enter the city through imposing Porta Aurea or Golden Gates built initially as triumphal arch of emperor Theodosius I in 391 This was the route Byzantine emperors took when leaving for campaign or returning to the city in triumph It was also the starting point for the Mese main avenue that would take the traveler past several fora and triumphal arches all the way to the heart of Constantinople the grand cathedral of Hagia Sophia Hippodrome and Great Palace Besides the monumental Golden Gates nine more gates pierced both the outer and inner walls used by civilians and the military Theodosian Walls were the most important defense of Constantinople As such the land walls were constantly maintained upgraded and extended The most significant extension happened in 11th Century during the reign of Komnenian emperors who built a whole new section of the wall to protect the Blachernae Palace near Golden Horn Besides land walls Sea Walls protected Constantinople from naval attack and offered additional protection to the ships in the city s principal harbor s on Sea of Marmara Lastly Anastasian Wall also known as Long Wall of Thrace located around 60km from city enclosed the peninsula providing first line of defense However fortification s length of 56km made it difficult to man significantly limiting its effectiveness

Constantinople but was it truly a university and was it really a continuous institution The dual role of politician and scholar stemmed from the nature of Byzantine higher education Since the year 360 holders of the highest posts in the imperial secretariat had been required by law to have completed a course of higher education and promotions were promised to those who attained distinction in the liberal arts There was what might be termed a university in Constantinople from at least 425 when it was reformed with thirty one chairs although it is perhaps misleading to use that word to describe it It was by no means an independent academy dedicated to the pursuit of learning for its own sake Its main aim was the production of able administrators It also lacked a corporate identity or name as it consisted of ad hoc appointments of teachers supported by the emperors Inevitably there were times when the university flourished and others when it was probably in abeyance It is impossible to document its continuous existence after c 600 what we have instead are periodic refoundations There is no evidence for its existence during the eighth century but it was revived during the reign of Michael III 842 867 The emperor s uncle the kaisar Bardas who largely ran the empire reestablished the university in the palace of the Magnaura part of the Great Palace complex There were to be teachers of philosophy grammar i e literature astronomy and geometry and they were to be paid from the treasury rather than be reliant on fees or bribes from students The philosophy teacher was Leo the Mathematician the most prominent Byzantine scholar of the time In 1045 the university was again revived and reformed faculties of Philosophy and Law were created with Constantine later Michael Psellos taking charge of Philosophy with the title Consul of the Philosophers and John Xiphilinos of Law as nomophylax Guardian of the Laws These two men were also close imperial advisors and played a direct role in making and implementing policy The capture and sack of Constantinople by the Fourth Crusade in 1204 brought about another hiatus although there is evidence that traditional higher education did continue on a smaller scale at the court in exile at Nicaea After the recapture of Constantinople in 1261 Michael VIII Palaiologos 1259 1282 refounded the university once more and entrusted its governance to George Akropolites one of his high ministers Higher education remained available in Constantinople until the city fell to the Ottoman Turks in 1453 although toward the end it was probably not funded from the treasury but by private fees By the mid fourteenth century Constantinople had lost its monopoly on higher education That was largely the result of the decentralization of power As Byzantine territory shrank and parts of the empire were cut off from Constantinople by land regional centers tended to be ruled almost autonomously by a junior member of the imperial family Between 1349 and 1380 the Byzantine holdings in the Peloponnese were administered by Manuel Kantakouzenos who resided in the town of Mistra and bore the title of despot Thessalonike too had a series of autonomous rulers starting with empress Anna the mother of John V Palaiologos 1341 1391 The courts of these provincial despots employed educated administrators and so generated the higher schooling that produced them The classical scholar Demetrios Triklinios ran a school in Thessalonike and the Platonist philosopher George Gemistos Plethon drew students to study under him at Mistra Source The Cambridge Intellectual History of Byzantium Ch 1 by Jonathan Harris
