ODO OF METZ THE ARMENIAN ARCHITECT AT THE HEART OF CHARLEMAGNE S EUROPE In the age of Charlemagne when Western Europe was emerging from the shadows of late antiquity and beginning what historians would later call the Carolingian Renaissance a mysterious master appeared at the center of the imperial court His name was Odo of Metz Eudes of Metz Oton Matsaetsi Almost nothing is known about his life Yet his name survived because of one extraordinary achievement he was credited with designing the monumental Palatine Chapel at Aachen the imperial church of Charlemagne A medieval inscription remembered him as the excellent master Odo And behind this mysterious architect lies a fascinating possibility A long standing tradition identifies Odo as Armenian in origin This cannot be established with absolute certainty from surviving contemporary records But the tradition is not without historical foundation Odo s origins are obscure while his architecture has long attracted comparisons with the centralized and domed churches of the Christian East including Armenian architectural traditions THE PALATINE CHAPEL OF AACHEN Beginning around 792 Charlemagne ordered the construction of his imperial palace complex at Aachen At its heart rose an extraordinary octagonal chapel consecrated in 805 The structure was unlike anything previously seen north of the Alps Its monumental octagon central dome galleries and sophisticated masonry created an imperial space whose ambition was unmistakable Charlemagne wanted Aachen to rival the great Christian capitals of the East and Rome The chapel drew heavily upon Late Antique and Byzantine architectural traditions particularly the famous Basilica of San Vitale in Ravenna Yet the building also demonstrates how architectural ideas could travel across the Christian world be transformed and emerge in entirely new forms in the Carolingian West And this is where the Armenian connection becomes particularly intriguing Armenian architecture had already developed highly sophisticated centralized churches centuries earlier The seventh century Zvartnots Cathedral and Saint Hripsime Church demonstrated an extraordinary mastery of domes centralized plans geometric organization and monumental stone construction Some historians and architectural scholars have therefore argued that Odo s work should be considered within the wider transmission of Eastern architectural ideas and have specifically proposed Armenian connections The case is especially interesting at Germigny des Pr s a Carolingian oratory built in 806 for Theodulf of Orl ans Its unusual centralized Greek cross design and eastern architectural character have repeatedly been compared with Armenian churches such as Etchmiadzin and Bagaran and Odo of Metz has traditionally been proposed as its architect FROM ARMENIA TO THE CAROLINGIAN WORLD Whether Odo himself was Armenian or whether Armenian architectural knowledge reached him through the wider Christian East the larger historical picture is extraordinary The medieval world was not a collection of isolated civilizations Ideas traveled Architects traveled Monks scholars craftsmen and manuscripts crossed mountains seas and empires Armenia stood at one of the great crossroads between the civilizations of the Mediterranean Persia and the Christian East Its architects had developed monumental traditions of stone construction and centralized church design long before Charlemagne s empire rose in Western Europe And centuries later in the heart of Charlemagne s imperial capital a mysterious master named Odo created one of the defining monuments of the European Middle Ages The Palatine Chapel of Aachen would become a symbol of imperial Europe Charlemagne was buried there in 814 and later German kings and emperors would be crowned in the chapel for centuries Thus whether we describe Odo as definitively Armenian or more cautiously as an architect traditionally associated with Armenian origins his story opens a remarkable window into the movement of knowledge between East and West From the stone churches of the Armenian Highlands to the imperial court of Charlemagne from the architectural traditions of the Christian East to the foundations of medieval European architecture Odo of Metz stands at one of the most fascinating crossroads in the history of European civilization A forgotten master An enigmatic architect And perhaps an Armenian hand that helped shape the architectural face of Charlemagne s Europe

August is named after the Roman emperor Augustus Born on September 23 63 BCE in a modest house on the Palatine Hill in Rome he was a sickly boy from a provincial family who grew up to become the most powerful human being the ancient world had ever produced He transformed a dying republic into an empire that lasted fifteen hundred years inaugurated two centuries of peace across three continents and left such an indelible mark on civilization that even the calendar the most fundamental organizing structure of human life still bears his name August is not just a month it is a monument carved not in stone but in time itself outlasting every statue temple and triumphal arch that the man it honors ever built Before it was August the month was called Sextilis Latin for the sixth This name made perfect sense in the original Roman calendar a ten month system traditionally attributed to Romulus the legendary founder of Rome That system began in March and ended in December with roughly sixty days of uncounted winter darkness between December and the next March that the Romans simply did not bother to name In this framework the months after June were named for their numerical position in the sequence Quintilis was the fifth month Sextilis the sixth September the seventh October the eighth November the ninth and December the tenth These numerical names are still embedded in our modern calendar though they no longer correspond to their original positions September the seventh month is now the ninth October the eighth is now the tenth November the ninth is now the eleventh and December the tenth is now the twelfth The calendar has been reformed expanded and reshuffled multiple times across two and a half millennia but the Latin numbers persist like fossils in the language remaining as reminders of an older system that no longer governs but still echoes The first major reform came around 713 BCE when Numa Pompilius the second legendary king of Rome added two new months Ianuarius named after Janus the two faced god of doorways and beginnings and Februarius named after Februa the Roman festival of purification These additions filled the winter gap and brought the calendar closer to the solar year Numa placed these new months before March pushing every subsequent month two positions forward Sextilis which had been the sixth month became the eighth yet it kept its old name For seven centuries the Romans called their eighth month the sixth without any apparent sense of contradiction because Roman culture was deeply conservative about names Once a thing was named it stayed named even when the label no longer made sense Then came Julius Caesar In 46 BCE Julius Caesar dictator of Rome conqueror of Gaul and the man who crossed the Rubicon to shatter the republic undertook the most ambitious calendar reform in Roman history Working with the Alexandrian astronomer Sosigenes Caesar replaced the old lunar calendar with a solar calendar of 365 days including a leap year every four years This Julian calendar was so accurate that it remained in use across the Western world for over 1 600 years until Pope Gregory XIII introduced the Gregorian calendar in 1582 Even then the Gregorian reform was a modification of Caesar s system not a replacement We still live in essence within the calendar that Julius Caesar built After Caesar s assassination on the Ides of March in 44 BCE the Roman Senate renamed the month of Quintilis the month in which Caesar had been born as Julius in his honor This became our July The precedent was set a month could be renamed for a man the calendar could be inscribed with the identity of a ruler and time itself could be made to carry a political message It was only a matter of time before someone else claimed the same honor That someone was Gaius Octavius Caesar s grand nephew and adopted heir A young man of eighteen when Caesar was murdered Octavius inherited not a throne but a civil war He spent the next thirteen years fighting manipulating and outmaneuvering every rival until he stood alone as the undisputed ruler of the Roman world His story is one of the most extraordinary in human history defined by patience calculation ruthlessness and political genius that has been studied by leaders dictators and statesmen for two thousand years When Caesar was assassinated Octavius was a teenager studying in Apollonia in modern day Albania He had no army no political base no administrative experience and no obvious claim to power beyond the fact that Caesar s will named him as adoptive son and heir Against him stood Mark Antony Caesar s most powerful lieutenant who controlled the legions and the treasury Lepidus another senior general Brutus and Cassius the leaders of the assassination conspiracy who commanded armies in the east and the entire apparatus of the Roman Senate which viewed the eighteen year old heir with a mixture of contempt and suspicion No one expected him to survive Cicero the greatest orator of the age famously planned to use the boy as a tool against Antony and then discard him remarking that the young man should be praised honored and removed In the end it was Cicero who was removed His name appeared on the proscription lists and his head and hands were nailed to the Rostra in the Forum by order of the young man he had underestimated Octavius formed the Second Triumvirate with Antony and Lepidus a formal alliance that divided the Roman world among the three men Together they defeated Brutus and Cassius at the Battle of Philippi in 42 BCE avenging Caesar s murder Then Octavius turned on his allies He marginalized Lepidus stripping him of power and sending him into comfortable exile He maneuvered Antony into an increasingly untenable position in the east where Antony s alliance with Cleopatra VII of Egypt provided Octavius with the perfect propaganda weapon a Roman general who had abandoned Roman values fallen under the spell of an eastern queen and planned to give Roman territories to foreign children Whether this narrative was entirely true was irrelevant it was effective In 31 BCE at the Battle of Actium off the western coast of Greece Octavius s fleet commanded by his brilliant general Marcus Agrippa destroyed the combined forces of Antony and Cleopatra They fled to Alexandria and Octavius followed In August of 30 BCE both Antony and Cleopatra took their own lives rather than be paraded through Rome in chains Egypt the wealthiest kingdom in the Mediterranean the breadbasket of the ancient world and the last of the great Hellenistic kingdoms became a Roman province Octavius was thirty three years old and he was the master of the world In 27 BCE Octavius performed the most brilliant political act of his career and perhaps in all of Western history He went before the Roman Senate and announced that he was surrendering his extraordinary powers to restore the republic The Senate terrified of a return to civil war and deeply aware that Octavius controlled every legion in the Roman world begged him to stay They showered him with titles and honors granted him command over the most important provinces and gave him tribunician power which made his person sacrosanct and granted him veto authority over any act of government They also gave him the name by which history would know him Augustus The name came from the Latin augere meaning to increase or to make sacred It carried connotations of religious authority moral grandeur and divine favor He was no longer Octavius the politician he was Augustus the revered the majestic and the one who augments and sanctifies Augustus did not call himself emperor He called himself princeps or first citizen He maintained the forms of the republic while emptying them of content The Senate still met magistrates were still elected and laws were still debated but everyone understood that ultimate authority rested with one man Augustus had invented a system that would endure for centuries an autocracy disguised as a republic a dictatorship wrapped in the ceremonies of democracy and a one man rule so skillfully constructed that Rome s governing class could participate without feeling they had surrendered their dignity This was his true genius seen not in battlefield victories which were mostly won by Agrippa but in the political architecture which was entirely his own The achievements that followed were staggering in scope Augustus reorganized the provinces establishing a clear distinction between senatorial provinces governed by the Senate and imperial provinces governed by his own appointees He created Rome s first standing professional army a permanent force of approximately 300 000 men stationed in frontier provinces paid regular salaries and granted land upon retirement This ended the cycle of civil wars that had been fueled by generals raising personal armies from unemployed veterans He established the Praetorian Guard as the emperor s personal bodyguard and the Vigiles as Rome s first professional fire brigade and police force He rebuilt Rome itself famously claiming that he had found a city of brick and left a city of marble The Forum of Augustus the Temple of Mars Ultor the Ara Pacis and the Mausoleum of Augustus were not merely buildings but statements of a new era and physical embodiments of a peace and prosperity that Rome had not known in a century And then there was the Pax Romana the Roman Peace Beginning with Augustus s consolidation of power after Actium and lasting approximately two hundred years the Pax Romana was the longest period of sustained peace and stability in the history of the Western world until the modern era Trade flourished across an empire that stretched from Britain to Egypt and from Spain to Syria Famous Roman roads engineered to last millennia connected every corner of the empire A common currency a common legal system and a common language of administration created an integrated economic and cultural zone of unprecedented scale The population of the empire reached approximately 60 million people as cities grew agriculture expanded and art literature and architecture flourished The Augustan age produced Virgil who wrote the Aeneid Rome s national epic modeled on Homer s Iliad and Odyssey It produced Horace Ovid Livy and Propertius driving a cultural flowering that would define Western civilization s understanding of classical antiquity for two thousand years In 8 BCE the Roman Senate decreed that the month of Sextilis would be renamed Augustus in honor of the emperor The Senate s decree was specific about why this particular month was chosen It stated that in Sextilis Augustus had first been admitted to the consulship In Sextilis he had celebrated three triumphs entering Rome in a triumphal procession which was the highest honor a Roman commander could receive In Sextilis the legions on the Janiculum Hill had placed themselves under his authority Egypt had been brought under the authority of the Roman people and an end had been put to the civil wars The month was not chosen arbitrarily it was chosen because it was the period in which Augustus s most consequential achievements had occurred It was the month in which the old world of civil war republican dysfunction and political chaos had ended and the new world of the Pax Romana had begun There is a popular myth that Augustus added days to his month to make it equal in length to July Caesar s month The story goes that he stole days from February to ensure that August had 31 days matching July s total because his ego would not tolerate his month being shorter than his adoptive father s This story while entertaining is false The distribution of days in the Julian calendar was established by Caesar himself and Sextilis already had 31 days before it was renamed Augustus did not need to inflate his month as it was already the same length as Caesar s Augustus died on August 19 14 CE at the age of seventy five in the town of Nola near Naples His last words according to the historian Suetonius were addressed to his wife Livia Have I played the part well Then applaud as I exit It was a theatrical metaphor from a man who had spent his entire life performing the role of first citizen performing the restoration of the republic and performing as the humble servant of the state while holding absolute power He had played the part so well that the empire he built survived in various forms for another fifteen hundred years in the west and nearly another fifteen hundred years in the east where the Byzantine Empire did not fall until Constantinople was conquered in 1453 Two thousand years later every human civilization on Earth that uses the Gregorian calendar marks its eighth month with the name of this man August not Sextilis or the eighth month remains Every legal document birth certificate death certificate contract treaty newspaper dateline and historical record that falls within the thirty one days of this month carries within it embedded in a single word the memory of a sickly boy from the Palatine Hill He outmaneuvered every rival ended a century of civil wars built an empire that reshaped the world and left his name not merely on a building or a statue but on time itself Empires fall statues crumble temples become ruins and triumphal arches weather into anonymity The calendar however endures As long as human beings count their days and name their months Augustus will be remembered not because historians chose to remember him or because schools teach his story or because monuments preserve his image but because every year without fail the eighth month arrives and the world without thinking speaks his name

Why Was Beijing Built Here Why did one of the world s great capitals rise at this particular spot The answer lies in a rare geographic combination Mountains to defend it A plain to sustain it Passes to the steppe Routes to the rest of China Beijing was chosen by geography and repeatedly chosen by history Beijing To Be Continued No 001 01 A City Between Mountains and Plain Look at a relief map of Beijing The Taihang mountain system rises to the west The Yan Mountains arc across the north To the south and east the land opens into the vast North China Plain Beijing is not enclosed by mountains It is partly sheltered by them while remaining open to the agricultural heartland 02 A Meeting Point of Several Worlds For an ancient capital this was an unusually powerful position South lay China s densely populated agricultural heartland North lay the Mongolian Plateau and the steppe East led toward Liaodong and Manchuria Westward routes crossed the Taihang Mountains Beijing stood where several geographic and cultural worlds met 03 The Gates Through the Mountains The mountains protected Beijing but did not completely seal it off Passes such as Juyong Gubeikou and Nankou allowed soldiers merchants and migrants to move between the Beijing Plain and the northern steppe Whoever controlled these corridors held the northern approaches to the city Beijing was both a gateway and a fortress guarding that gateway 04 Why Vulnerability Created Value Beijing s location was also dangerous A capital farther south might be safer from northern invasion but less able to control the frontier Beijing was close enough to watch the steppe yet connected enough to govern the agricultural regions farther south Its vulnerability was inseparable from its strategic value 05 The Problem of Water Then there was water The Yongding River entered the plain from the western mountains The Chaobai river system shaped the northeast and east Springs lakes and wetlands once dotted the region Yet Beijing was never naturally blessed with unlimited water Every dynasty that enlarged the city had to engineer its survival 06 A Capital Must Be Fed Canals reservoirs wells and diverted springs supplied the growing population The Grand Canal brought another essential resource grain from southern China A capital might survive an attack behind high walls It could not survive long without food and water Beijing s history is therefore also a history of hydraulic engineering and long distance supply 07 The First City Was Elsewhere Beijing s earliest urban center was not located around today s Forbidden City The ancient city of Ji stood farther southwest probably near today s Guang anmen and Lotus Pond area Its location offered access to water and important north south routes Only centuries later would Beijing s urban heart move northeast 08 Beijing and the World c 1045 BCE Chinese historical tradition places Ji around the beginning of the Western Zhou era Classical Greece had not yet reached its great age Rome s traditional founding date 753 BCE was still almost three centuries away In Africa Egypt s New Kingdom was nearing its end Beijing was already ancient but it was not yet an imperial capital 09 From Ji to Youzhou Under the Qin and Han empires Ji remained an important northern administrative and military center During the Sui and Tang periods the region was generally known as Youzhou Its main role was not to govern the entire empire It was to defend the empire s northern approaches and connect the Central Plains with the frontier 10 The Liao Southern Capital In 938 the Liao dynasty made the city its Southern Capital or Nanjing not to be confused with the modern city of Nanjing At roughly the same time Europe was in the early Middle Ages Constantinople remained the center of the Byzantine Empire and the Fatimids would establish Cairo in 969 Beijing had entered the world of dynastic capitals 11 The Rise of Jin Zhongdu The decisive transformation came in 1153 The Jin dynasty moved its principal capital here and named it Zhongdu the Central Capital For the first time Beijing became the main capital of a dynasty ruling much of northern China The city still lay southwest of today s historic center near the Guang anmen area 12 Beijing and the World c 1153 While Jin Zhongdu was rising the Crusades continued in the Mediterranean world and the age of Gothic cathedrals was beginning Notre Dame de Paris would be started in 1163 In southern Africa Great Zimbabwe was developing into a major political and trading center Across continents cities were expressing new forms of wealth belief and power 13 The Destruction of Zhongdu Jin Zhongdu was devastated during the Mongol conquest in 1215 Half a century later Kublai Khan chose not to rebuild entirely on its ruins Instead he constructed a new capital farther northeast close to the lakes around Jishuitan Large scale construction of Dadu began around 1267 The center of Beijing moved 14 Why Kublai Khan Moved Northeast One major reason was water The lakes around Jishuitan could supply the city and connect it to an expanded canal system Under the engineer Guo Shoujing waterways helped grain shipments reach the Yuan capital Palaces displayed imperial power Canals lakes and grain ships kept that power alive 15 Beijing and the World c 1267 As Yuan Dadu took shape Baghdad was recovering from its capture by Mongol forces in 1258 European cities and trade were reviving Marco Polo began his journey east in 1271 In Africa the Mali Empire was rising while Great Zimbabwe linked gold producing regions with Indian Ocean trade Dadu belonged to an age of expanding connections across Eurasia and beyond 16 The Birth of Ming Beijing In 1403 the Yongle Emperor renamed Beiping Beijing the Northern Capital He rebuilt and enlarged the city with a new imperial palace walls gates and ritual complexes In 1421 Beijing formally became the principal capital of the Ming dynasty The Forbidden City Temple of Heaven and the mature central axis plan emerged from this transformation 17 Beijing and the Renaissance World As Ming Beijing took shape Renaissance Florence was flourishing Brunelleschi was beginning the great dome of Florence Cathedral In Africa Great Zimbabwe remained an important center while Timbuktu was approaching its golden age of scholarship and trans Saharan trade Beijing s monumental transformation was part of a wider age of ambitious cities 18 The Geography That Endured Beijing remained the capital through the Ming and Qing dynasties It became Beiping during part of the Republican era then was established as the capital of the People s Republic of China in 1949 Its scale walls and technology changed dramatically Its underlying geographic logic did not END A City Still Being Written Mountains still rise to Beijing s west and north The plain still opens south and east Northern passes still lead toward the steppe while roads railways and waterways connect the city with the rest of China So why was Beijing built here Because the mountains made it defensible The plain gave it room and access to food Rivers canals and wells allowed it to survive Its position connected the Chinese heartland the northern frontier the steppe and Northeast Asia No single emperor simply chose Beijing For three thousand years geography war trade water and political ambition kept choosing it again Beijing is a city selected by mountains and rivers and rebuilt by generation after generation Beijing To Be Continued No 001

My 2 cents The term Palestine has a complex history that has evolved over millennia In ancient times the land was inhabited by a variety of peoples including the Philistines Hebrews and others The name Palestine likely has its origins from the word Philistia referring to the Philistines Under the Roman Empire after the suppression of the Jewish revolts the province of Judaea was renamed Syria Palaestina in an attempt to minimize Jewish identification with the land Over the subsequent centuries the area changed hands among various empires including the Byzantine Islamic Caliphates Crusaders Ottoman Turks and most recently the British The British Mandate for Palestine established after World War I brought the term back into modern usage and it was during this period that the Zionist movement advocated for the establishment of a Jewish homeland in Palestine With the creation of the State of Israel in 1948 the term Palestinian increasingly came to refer to the Arab population in the West Bank and Gaza Strip as well as those who became refugees

Kharanah Palace Qasr al Kharanah one of Jordan s most famous desert castles dates back to the early Umayyad era around the early 8th Century CE situated in the arid expanse of the eastern Jordanian desert it is one of several desert castles built by the Umayyads for both practical and ceremonial purposes The palace s design a rectangular fortress with four corner towers blends Roman Byzantine and early Islamic architectural influences reflecting the cultural fusion of its time Despite its fortress like appearance Kharanah Palace was not primarily military but likely served as a caravanserai rest stop or meeting place for tribal leaders and officials Its two story structure contains about 60 rooms arranged around a central courtyard showcasing advanced engineering for ventilation and light in a desert climate Inscriptions found on the walls written in early Arabic script have helped historians date the structure to around 710 CE during the reign of Caliph al Walid I The thick limestone walls and small windows were designed to withstand the harsh desert environment offering cool shelter amid the surrounding barrenness Kharanah Palace s precise purpose remains partly mysterious adding to its allure as an archaeological enigma of early Islamic world It stands today as one of the best preserved Umayyad desert castles along with Qasr Amra and Qasr al Azraq forming part of Jordan s rich early Islamic heritage trail Now protected and celebrated as a symbol of early Islamic architecture Kharanah Palace continues to captivate visitors with its stark beauty and echoes of a distant desert empire camera Credit to the Owner

Acacius of Byzantium also sometimes known as Agathus is a figure steeped in the rich tapestry of Byzantine history His life and subsequent canonisation are fascinating subjects worthy of exploration Born in the 3rd century AD in the Byzantine Empire Acacius was a soldier by profession but his life changed dramatically due to his profound faith in Christianity which was then considered a minority and persecuted religion in the Roman Empire Acacius was part of the Roman army stationed in Mauretania modern day Algeria and Morocco His faith was a powerful part of his life even as he served in the Roman army He was not shy to express his beliefs and was known for his piety and devotion However such dedication to Christianity was not without its hardships During the reign of Emperor Maximian a severe persecution of Christians was underway Acacius refused to sacrifice to the pagan gods a standard practice in the Roman army and was therefore subjected to various tortures Despite the severity of these punishments Acacius remained steadfast in his faith His courage and devotion inspired many of his fellow soldiers leading them to convert to Christianity He was eventually beheaded for his refusal to renounce his faith thus becoming a martyr His death was not in vain however as it sparked a wave of conversions and strengthened the resolve of existing Christians As the story of his courage devotion and martyrdom spread Acacius was revered by the Christian community His canonisation however was not an immediate process Canonisation in the early Christian church was a local matter often initiated by popular devotion rather than by a formal process The local Christian community recognised Acacius as a saint due to his martyrdom and the miracles that were reported at his tomb It was not until the 10th century almost seven centuries after his death that Acacius of Byzantium was officially canonised by the church His feast day was established on May 8 and his veneration spread beyond Byzantium to the wider Christian world Today he is recognised as a saint in both the Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic churches The life and canonisation of Acacius of Byzantium present a compelling narrative of faith courage and resilience His is a story of a soldier who chose faith over compliance a man who held on to his beliefs even in the face of death His martyrdom and the subsequent canonisation serve as a testament to the power of faith and the impact one individual can have on the course of religious history Though the process of canonisation took centuries the legacy and memory of Acacius have endured making him an enduring figure of Christian devotion and steadfastness His story serves as an inspiration to those who face adversity demonstrating the power of unwavering belief and the potential for one person s faith to inspire others God bless and may He continue to bless the GREAT nation of Australia

The Feast of All Saints in the Christian East and West The Christian East and West once shared overlapping traditions for the commemoration of the martyrs and saints although the history is more complex than saying that the entire Church originally observed one universal date and that the West later simply changed it Different local churches developed commemorations at different times and these customs gradually became more standardized Early commemorations in the Christian East The earliest forms of what became the Feast of All Saints appear to have been collective commemorations of the martyrs Saint Ephrem the Syrian c 306 373 bears witness to an early common commemoration of martyrs in the Syriac Christian tradition Another important tradition developed at Antioch where the martyrs were commemorated on the Sunday after Pentecost Saint John Chrysostom c 347 407 while serving at Antioch preached a homily for a collective commemoration of the martyrs associated with the Sunday following Pentecost This provides particularly important evidence for the antiquity of the Eastern observance Over time the commemoration expanded beyond the martyrs to embrace all the saints Apostles Prophets Hierarchs Martyrs Confessors Monastics and all righteous men and women known and unknown The Orthodox Church in Eastern Rite use continues to celebrate the Sunday of All Saints on the first Sunday after Pentecost Liturgically this placement has a theological significance Pentecost manifests the descent and activity of the Holy Spirit while All Saints celebrates the sanctification of human beings accomplished through that same Holy Spirit Early commemorations in the Christian West The West likewise developed collective commemorations of the martyrs A major development occurred under Pope Saint Boniface IV pope 608 615 In 609 or 610 the Byzantine emperor Phocas granted the Pantheon in Rome to Boniface who converted the former pagan temple into a Christian church dedicated to the Blessed Virgin Mary and All the Martyrs Sancta Maria ad Martyres The dedication was celebrated on 13 May and its anniversary became an important Roman commemoration of the martyrs Saint Boniface IV himself is recognized as a saint in the Western tradition The relationship between the Roman May 13 observance and earlier Eastern commemorations on or around that date is difficult to establish with certainty The resemblance is noteworthy but it is safer to speak of overlapping Eastern and Western traditions rather than to claim confidently that Rome simply borrowed the date from the East Thus during the centuries of the undivided Church Christians in East and West possessed several related traditions for collectively honoring the martyrs and eventually all the saints The emergence of November 1 in the Orthodox West The Western Orthodox observance gradually became associated with November 1 Under Pope Saint Gregory III 731 741 an oratory was established within Old St Peter s Basilica in Rome and dedicated to the Apostles and to the saints martyrs confessors and righteous throughout the world The anniversary associated with this Roman observance came to be celebrated on November 1 The precise origin of November 1 is not completely certain Similar observances appear in the early medieval churches of the British Isles and the Frankish world and historians have consequently debated whether the November date originated at Rome or whether Rome adopted or reinforced a practice already developing elsewhere in Western Europe Pope Gregory IV 827 844 subsequently encouraged the wider observance of the November 1 feast during the reign of the Carolingian emperor Louis the Pious 778 840 Gregory instructed Louis to proclaim to go back to the earlier medieval history to the time when the Holy Roman Empire was formed following the reign of Charlemagne and its later revival by Otto the Great 9 11th centuries At the time the Holy Roman Emperor had the most prestigious title in Latin Christendom The title of king was inferior used in similar manner how the Romans referred to client kings Such arrangement was recognized by the Church which wanted to imitate the Byzantine Empire in the West Even though Holy Roman Emperors never came close to ruling over entire Latin Christendom they still defined themselves in the terms of being vested with the dominium mundi just like the Pope This ultimately led to clash between these two in the form of Investiture Controversy starting in 11th century Over the next centuries the power of the Emperor weakened and that of the Pope grew This coincided with the beginning of Crusades which were an important symbol of papal supremacy as the popes were able to direct military campaigns against both external and internal enemies of the Christendom This effectively meant that the Pope commanded an invisible empire of various Catholic nobles and institutions over Christendom which responded to his call and feared excommunication The doctrines of rightful expansion of this Christendom were formed during this time and would later serve as the foundation of Spanish conquest of the Aztecs However there was an another important development in the subsequent centuries where individual Catholic states monarchies started to grow in power through the means of centralizing institutions and kings acquiring more power and prestige This led to the development of the concept that the King is the emperor in his kingdom Rex est imperator in regno suo and from 14th century on this became regularly used What this effectively meant is that the powerful European kings such as the King of France considered themselves to be on equal terms with the Emperor As the prestige of the Holy Roman Emperor faded the Latin Christendom basically became a commonwealth of Catholic states headed by the Pope who was recognized as the universal power and its spiritual authority By the end of 15th century when the Treaty of Tordesillas was signed the Latin Christendom consisted of increasingly more centralized and powerful kingdoms like Portugal Spain France and England The expansionism of Portugal and Spain was not based on an actual imperial ideology but was legitimized by the pope so it was in a way actually anti imperial The imperialism in 16th century context would be if the King of Castile would consider himself as the Emperor with his own dominium mundi equal to that of the pope The funny thing is that Castile would later actually become ruled by the person who also happened to be Holy Roman Emperor Charles V but he ruled over the New World as the King of Castile not as the Holy Roman Emperor So when we re talking about 16th century Spanish Empire we re actually talking about a kingdom a monarchy The term empire is now unfortunately used in a completely different way where it essentially means something along the likes of a large state This development comes from the centuries that followed With the Protestant Reformation the Catholic Christendom effectively fell apart and the authority of the Pope diminished Politics began to revolve around the balance of power of increasingly more centralized and sovereign European states Protestant states such as England Dutch Republic etc defined their own sovereignty independent of the Pope and began conquering the world without needing his blessing France too started its own project of conquering lands in New World ignoring the Treaty of Tordesillas despite being a Catholic kingdom The 16th century King of France Francis I famously said on this issue The sun shines for me as it does for others I would very much like to see the clause of Adam s will by which I should be denied my share of the world So what effectively followed from around mid 16th century onward was these powerful European states started to do their own thing staging pirate attacks and raid on each other s colonies eventually establishing what we now call overseas empires and going after each other fighting all over the world It was not uncommon that in this spectacle of worldwide war and violence Europeans allied with non Europeans and fought against other coalitions of Europeans and non Europeans throwing any sort of allegiance to common Christendom out of the window The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 is often seen as marking the beginning of the new era of international relations and sovereignty From that point on we can indeed talk about Europeans rather than just Christendom To sum it up at the time when the Spanish started conquering the New World there was still a commonwealth of Christendom headed by the Pope who gave them the legitimacy to do it But as Christendom collapsed between Catholics and Protestant the individual states started engaging in what would eventually become secular diplomacy ignoring the old religious concepts and hierarchy With Napoleonic Wars the Holy Roman Empire officially disappeared and Napoleon himself gave a new meaning to the term emperor when he crowned himself as one despite not embracing any of the old ideological implications of this term The term empire basically became a rhetorical embellishment and was used by 19th century states such as the French Empire the German Empire and the Austrian Empire None of these states disputed each other s title of empire which they should have if they followed the original idea of empire where there could only be one universal emperor This evolution is what would eventually led to the use of term imperialism in late 19th century to describe aggressive expansionist actions of individual states So when we talk about imperialism now we re talking about something very modern which doesn t really mean anything in early 16th century context The problem of this type of imperialism of European states has to be understood by the de facto disappearance of a supreme spiritual authority over entire Europe like the Pope which eventually resulted in European states engaging in unregulated global struggle for supremacy inhibited only by fragile balance of power This eventually led to modern anti imperialism in the form of various concepts as well as imposing an international order to prevent aggressive wars of conquest So the discussion between imperialism and anti imperialism is a very modern one that can only really be used in a modern context What the Spanish did in the Americas when they conquered the Aztecs was a classic conquest that was an extension of medieval wars of religion and it was defined in medieval terms Condemning this on modern anti imperialist grounds is silly because no such concept even existed at the time Cultures across the world supported what we call the Right of Conquest When various people over the world fought against the Spanish they were not doing this from anti imperialist grounds they were doing this for their own interest There was no concept of a world in which conquest is wrong by default and all the states should just stay within their borders This is a totally modern concept and by modern I mean like 20th century For example I understand people condemning things like slavery or various massacres because the opposition to slavery and indiscriminate killings existed at the time There were contemporaries criticizing these things The same goes for the treatment of natives which was also often criticized and discussed by legal theorists and theologians However condemning pre modern conquests as such in a world where the Right of Conquest was the norm accepted across civilization makes no sense There was literally no one among the learn who proposed a world in which no conquest should ever take place So there wasn t even any discussion on this Everybody understood that if you lost a war and got conquered the conqueror would rule over the territory and impose his law Of course people often fought against that even after the fact was done but they were doing it to impose their own state which would also believe in the right to conquer others These were the rules of the game For example when Muslims conquered Christian territories the Christians also didn t complain how conquests were unjust by default It was usually seen along the lines that this was a punishment for their sins and that the rule of non another as Pacific seaboard and the borderlands facing the kingdoms of Poland and Hungary As 13th Century CE progressed historic empires which until recently had asserted themselves confidently now lay in crumbled ruins This was a time of conquest and the Mongols were not gentle in imposing their rule Their armies left a trail of devastation in their wake filled with plundered cities piles of corpses and deserted settlements Once their armies had crushed all resistance Mongol governors sought to revive commerce rebuild industries and encourage prosperity Like so many conquerors they wanted to be able to extract taxation and perhaps more importantly ensure that everyone within their lands channelled their efforts towards Mongol Empire s ultimate goal governance over all human civilization To this end Mongols went to great lengths to recruit skilled artisans and merchants who could be of value to their empire Such individuals were often uprooted and transported for thousands of miles to locations where Mongols felt that they could be of greatest use Some including Venetian traveler Marco Polo entered Mongol Empire voluntarily offering their services as translators diplomats or merchants Mongols leaders considered intellectuals and scholars to be important assets and they generally sought to put them to work for the betterment of their empire In the 1260s Hulegu a Mongol commander and grandson of Genghis Khan established a research center for thinkers across Eurasia at a place called Maragha now located in East Azerbaijan Province of Iran Hulegu wanted these intellectuals to exercise their talents in his service and he was eager for them to devote themselves to the study of alchemy astrology and anything that might improve the lifespan or health of the reigning sultan Many of these goals were naturally unworkable and yet by assembling so many highly trained thinkers he paved the way for advances that would have a lasting impact especially in the field of trigonometry as George Lane shows in Early Mongol Rule in 13th Century Iran Hulagu also worked with the Persian astronomer Nasir al Din al Tusi to build the Maragha Observatory which was among the most advanced observatories in the world at the time Mongol Empire encouraged free trade and often took items from one country and introduced them to other countries world but it was in this period that it reached the Mediterranean and from there into Byzantine Empire Western Christendom and many parts of wider world Ahmad al Hassan points out in a 2003 study that some parts of the Muslim world already had access to gunpowder and its forbears Even so advent of the Mongol Empire seems to have substantially accelerated the diffusion of this technology While some military technologies were traveling westwards others were heading east During 1270s Mongol rulers in the Near East sent Muslim engineers capable of constructing advanced siege catapults into China to any diplomatic contact with China was established In 551 two Byzantine monks who had been preaching in India made their way to China and observed the intricate methods used in the raising of silkworms and the production of silk They hurried back to Constantinople and sought an urgent audience with the Emperor Justinian They told him that they had found the source of the miracle material silk and the emperor was impressed He offered them a great fortune if they were able to smuggle some of these mysterious worms back to the capital The monks set out once again likely travelling along a northern route along the Black Sea They would have passed through the Tarim Basin and the Taklamakan Desert through the Gate of Jade and down the Hexi Corridor into the heartlands of China With them they carried bamboo canes hollowed out on the inside with hidden compartments In China they convinced others to smuggle the silkworms out for them likely in the form of eggs or very young larvae since adult silkworms are very delicate and easily killed by temperature variations The entire expedition may have taken up to two years but they eventually returned successful and established a breeding population of silkworms on the other end of the Silk Road Their actions began a Byzantine trade in silk with silk factories setting up in Constantinople as well as Beirut Antioch and Thebes Byzantine traditions toward a unified Christian identity influencing law art architecture and education Volodymyr built churches promoted literacy and strengthened alliances through marriage and diplomacy His rule laid the groundwork for the cultural flourishing that followed He died on July 15 1015 near Kiev Later canonized as a saint by both the Eastern Orthodox and Catholic churches he is remembered as
